Concept & Climate-Informed Monoliths Light-Sculpted Mass bridges generative form-finding and environmental performance analysis within a single interactive Julia application. Calibrated to the equatorial solar geometry of Bandung, Indonesia (6.9175° S, 107.6191° E), the project investigates how monumental, monolithic architecture can be carved open by courtyards, deep entrance portals, roof terraces, and narrow vertical light slots—and how those spatial voids perform under tropical daylight.
Rather than treating massing generation and solar simulation as separate stages across different software packages, this custom tool integrates Constructive Solid Geometry (CSG) directly with an analytical solar ray-casting engine and a real-time evaluation dashboard.
The Computational Logic: Boolean CSG & Solar Ray-Casting As illustrated in the system diagram below, the software operates through two linked computational engines—first synthesizing the architectural solid-void composition, then evaluating its daily solar exposure across both building surfaces and the surrounding site:
Additive & Subtractive CSG Massing (Steps 01–04): Using a seeded generator (Seed 2026, Light Canyon family), the algorithm first assembles three interlocking rectangular volumes: a dominant base monolith (B₁), a taller secondary tower mass (B₂), and a cantilevered upper gallery (B₃). It then subtracts up to five spatial voids—an open-to-sky central courtyard (C₁), a monumental ground entrance (C₂), a recessed roof terrace (C₃), a narrow vertical light slot (C₄), and a lateral recess (C₅)—partitioning the resulting solid into an exact boundary mesh with crisp architectural edge lines. Equatorial Sun Position & Analytical Ray-Box Testing: For any selected date (such as 2026-11-22), the script calculates Bandung’s solar azimuth and elevation at 30-minute intervals from 05:00 to 19:00 WIB. Every building facade is subdivided into 3.0 m analytical patches and the surrounding site into a 2.5 m ground grid. From each sample point, solar rays are tested directly against the additive and subtractive CSG boxes to determine instantaneous shadows and cumulative daily direct sun hours (0 to 14 hours). Preliminary Design Evaluation (AMQI): It is important to note that the solar analysis evaluates the generated geometry rather than automatically optimizing it. To help the architect compare different random seeds, the dashboard computes a preliminary Architectural Massing Quality Index (AMQI = 61.8 / 100) that balances the solid-void ratio (22.1%), primary mass dominance, and average courtyard sun exposure (1.11 hours/day). View Julia Source Code (light_sculpted_mass.jl) using GLMakie using GeometryBasics using Random using Colors using Dates using Statistics # Define the geographic location const LATITUDE = -6.9175 const LONGITUDE = 107.6191 const UTC_OFFSET = 7.0 # Define the initial design settings const INITIAL_SEED = 2026 const INITIAL_DATE = Date(2026, 11, 22) const INITIAL_HOUR = 9 const INITIAL_MINUTE = 0 # Define the analytical grid resolution const GROUND_MIN = -80.0 const GROUND_MAX = 80.0 const GROUND_STEP = 2.5 const SURFACE_STEP = 3.0 # Define the daily solar analysis period const SUN_START_HOUR = 5 const SUN_END_HOUR = 19 const SUN_INTERVAL = 30 const MAX_SUN_HOURS = 14.0 # Define the architectural material const CONCRETE_COLOR = RGBf(0.80, 0.81, 0.79) const CONCRETE_DIFFUSE = Vec3f(0.85, 0.85, 0.85) const CONCRETE_SPECULAR = Vec3f(0.02, 0.02, 0.02) const CONCRETE_SHININESS = 8f0 # Define the analytical color palette const SOLAR_PALETTE = RGBf[ RGBf(0.13, 0.22, 0.50), RGBf(0.13, 0.50, 0.78), RGBf(0.28, 0.73, 0.62), RGBf(0.95, 0.79, 0.26), RGBf(0.83, 0.30, 0.18) ] const NEUTRAL_GROUND = RGBf(0.92, 0.91, 0.88) const SHADOW_COLOR = RGBf(0.44, 0.48, 0.52) const SUNLIT_COLOR = RGBf(0.92, 0.89, 0.83) # Define an axis-aligned architectural solid struct BoxVolume xmin::Float64 xmax::Float64 ymin::Float64 ymax::Float64 zmin::Float64 zmax::Float64 end # Create a solid from its center and dimensions function make_box(cx, cy, width, depth, zmin, zmax) return BoxVolume( cx - width / 2, cx + width / 2, cy - depth / 2, cy + depth / 2, zmin, zmax ) end # Check whether a point lies inside a solid function inside_box(x, y, z, box::BoxVolume) return ( box.xmin <= x <= box.xmax && box.ymin <= y <= box.ymax && box.zmin <= z <= box.zmax ) end # Evaluate the final constructive solid geometry function inside_solid(x, y, z, additions, cutters) occupied = any( b -> inside_box(x, y, z, b), additions ) if !occupied return false end removed = any( b -> inside_box(x, y, z, b), cutters ) return !removed end # Create an empty geometry container function new_geometry() return ( Point3f[], TriangleFace{Int}[] ) end # Add a quadrilateral surface function add_quad!(geo, a, b, c, d) vertices, faces = geo base = length(vertices) append!(vertices, Point3f[a, b, c, d]) push!( faces, TriangleFace(base + 1, base + 2, base + 3) ) push!( faces, TriangleFace(base + 1, base + 3, base + 4) ) return nothing end # Convert geometry into a renderable mesh function build_mesh(geo) return GeometryBasics.Mesh( geo[1], geo[2] ) end # Generate a monumental architectural composition function generate_architecture(seed) rng = MersenneTwister(seed) additions = BoxVolume[] cutters = BoxVolume[] # Select the architectural composition family composition = rand(rng, 1:4) names = ( "Carved Monolith", "Shifted Monoliths", "Terraced Monolith", "Light Canyon" ) # Generate the dominant primary mass base_width = rand(rng, 60.0:1.0:72.0) base_depth = rand(rng, 43.0:1.0:54.0) base_height = rand(rng, 22.0:1.0:30.0) push!( additions, make_box( 0.0, 0.0, base_width, base_depth, 0.0, base_height ) ) # Generate the secondary monolithic mass side = rand(rng, (-1.0, 1.0)) secondary_x = side * rand(rng, 13.0:1.0:21.0) secondary_y = rand(rng, 3.0:1.0:12.0) secondary_width = rand(rng, 28.0:1.0:37.0) secondary_depth = rand(rng, 30.0:1.0:41.0) secondary_height = rand(rng, 32.0:1.0:42.0) # Apply composition-specific transformations if composition == 2 secondary_x *= 1.30 secondary_y += 5.0 elseif composition == 3 secondary_height *= 1.15 elseif composition == 4 secondary_x *= 0.75 secondary_y += 7.0 end push!( additions, make_box( secondary_x, secondary_y, secondary_width, secondary_depth, 0.0, secondary_height ) ) # Generate a massive projecting gallery extension_level = rand(rng, 17.0:1.0:24.0) extension_x = -side * rand(rng, 10.0:1.0:18.0) extension_y = rand(rng, -11.0:1.0:-4.0) extension_width = rand(rng, 35.0:1.0:48.0) extension_depth = rand(rng, 23.0:1.0:33.0) extension_height = rand(rng, 11.0:1.0:17.0) if composition == 1 extension_x *= 1.15 elseif composition == 3 extension_level += 6.0 elseif composition == 4 extension_y -= 5.0 end push!( additions, make_box( extension_x, extension_y, extension_width, extension_depth, extension_level, extension_level + extension_height ) ) # Generate the central open-air courtyard courtyard_x = rand(rng, -8.0:1.0:8.0) courtyard_y = rand(rng, 1.0:1.0:8.0) courtyard_width = rand(rng, 15.0:1.0:23.0) courtyard_depth = rand(rng, 18.0:1.0:27.0) if composition == 2 courtyard_x += 7.0 * side elseif composition == 4 courtyard_width *= 0.75 courtyard_depth *= 1.25 end courtyard = make_box( courtyard_x, courtyard_y, courtyard_width, courtyard_depth, -1.0, 70.0 ) push!(cutters, courtyard) # Carve the monumental entrance entrance_width = rand(rng, 10.0:1.0:16.0) entrance_height = rand(rng, 12.0:1.0:19.0) entrance_y = courtyard_y - courtyard_depth / 2 - 11.0 push!( cutters, make_box( courtyard_x, entrance_y, entrance_width, 28.0, -1.0, entrance_height ) ) # Carve a large roof terrace terrace_x = -side * rand(rng, 20.0:1.0:28.0) terrace_y = rand(rng, 9.0:1.0:18.0) terrace_width = rand(rng, 19.0:1.0:26.0) terrace_depth = rand(rng, 18.0:1.0:27.0) terrace_level = rand(rng, 13.0:1.0:20.0) push!( cutters, make_box( terrace_x, terrace_y, terrace_width, terrace_depth, terrace_level, 70.0 ) ) # Carve a deep vertical light slot slot_x = secondary_x + rand(rng, -5.0:1.0:5.0) slot_y = secondary_y + rand(rng, -4.0:1.0:4.0) slot_width = rand(rng, 3.5:0.5:6.5) slot_depth = rand(rng, 16.0:1.0:25.0) slot_bottom = rand(rng, 11.0:1.0:18.0) push!( cutters, make_box( slot_x, slot_y, slot_width, slot_depth, slot_bottom, 70.0 ) ) # Generate one optional lateral recess if composition == 2 || composition == 4 push!( cutters, make_box( side * 30.0, rand(rng, -8.0:1.0:4.0), rand(rng, 15.0:1.0:22.0), rand(rng, 19.0:1.0:27.0), -1.0, rand(rng, 12.0:1.0:19.0) ) ) end return ( additions=additions, cutters=cutters, courtyard=courtyard, name=names[composition] ) end # Generate the CSG coordinate partitions function csg_partition(design) all_boxes = vcat( design.additions, design.cutters ) xs = sort(unique(vcat( [b.xmin for b in all_boxes], [b.xmax for b in all_boxes] ))) ys = sort(unique(vcat( [b.ymin for b in all_boxes], [b.ymax for b in all_boxes] ))) zs = sort(unique(vcat( [b.zmin for b in all_boxes], [b.zmax for b in all_boxes] ))) nx = length(xs) - 1 ny = length(ys) - 1 nz = length(zs) - 1 occupied = falses(nx, ny, nz) volume = 0.0 # Evaluate each partition cell for i in 1:nx, j in 1:ny, k in 1:nz cx = (xs[i] + xs[i+1]) / 2 cy = (ys[j] + ys[j+1]) / 2 cz = (zs[k] + zs[k+1]) / 2 occupied[i, j, k] = inside_solid( cx, cy, cz, design.additions, design.cutters ) if occupied[i, j, k] volume += (xs[i+1] - xs[i]) * (ys[j+1] - ys[j]) * (zs[k+1] - zs[k]) end end return ( xs=xs, ys=ys, zs=zs, occupied=occupied, volume=volume ) end # Subdivide a building face into analytical patches function add_surface_patches!( geo, centers, normals, areas, a, b, c, d, normal ) edge_u = sqrt(sum( (Float64(b[i]) - Float64(a[i]))^2 for i in 1:3 )) edge_v = sqrt(sum( (Float64(d[i]) - Float64(a[i]))^2 for i in 1:3 )) nu = max(1, ceil(Int, edge_u / SURFACE_STEP)) nv = max(1, ceil(Int, edge_v / SURFACE_STEP)) function point_at(u, v) return Point3f( a[1] + u * (b[1] - a[1]) + v * (d[1] - a[1]), a[2] + u * (b[2] - a[2]) + v * (d[2] - a[2]), a[3] + u * (b[3] - a[3]) + v * (d[3] - a[3]) ) end patch_area = edge_u * edge_v / (nu * nv) for i in 1:nu, j in 1:nv u1 = (i - 1) / nu u2 = i / nu v1 = (j - 1) / nv v2 = j / nv p1 = point_at(u1, v1) p2 = point_at(u2, v1) p3 = point_at(u2, v2) p4 = point_at(u1, v2) add_quad!(geo, p1, p2, p3, p4) center = point_at( (u1 + u2) / 2, (v1 + v2) / 2 ) push!( centers, ( Float64(center[1]), Float64(center[2]), Float64(center[3]) ) ) push!(normals, normal) push!(areas, patch_area) end return nothing end # Generate the external CSG building surfaces function generate_building_surfaces(design) partition = csg_partition(design) xs = partition.xs ys = partition.ys zs = partition.zs occupied = partition.occupied nx, ny, nz = size(occupied) geo = new_geometry() centers = NTuple{3,Float64}[] normals = NTuple{3,Float64}[] areas = Float64[] p(x, y, z) = Point3f(x, y, z) # Construct outward-facing boundary surfaces for i in 1:nx, j in 1:ny, k in 1:nz if !occupied[i, j, k] continue end x1, x2 = xs[i], xs[i+1] y1, y2 = ys[j], ys[j+1] z1, z2 = zs[k], zs[k+1] # Negative X face if i == 1 || !occupied[i-1, j, k] add_surface_patches!( geo, centers, normals, areas, p(x1, y1, z1), p(x1, y1, z2), p(x1, y2, z2), p(x1, y2, z1), (-1.0, 0.0, 0.0) ) end # Positive X face if i == nx || !occupied[i+1, j, k] add_surface_patches!( geo, centers, normals, areas, p(x2, y1, z1), p(x2, y2, z1), p(x2, y2, z2), p(x2, y1, z2), (1.0, 0.0, 0.0) ) end # Negative Y face if j == 1 || !occupied[i, j-1, k] add_surface_patches!( geo, centers, normals, areas, p(x1, y1, z1), p(x2, y1, z1), p(x2, y1, z2), p(x1, y1, z2), (0.0, -1.0, 0.0) ) end # Positive Y face if j == ny || !occupied[i, j+1, k] add_surface_patches!( geo, centers, normals, areas, p(x2, y2, z1), p(x1, y2, z1), p(x1, y2, z2), p(x2, y2, z2), (0.0, 1.0, 0.0) ) end # Bottom face if k == 1 || !occupied[i, j, k-1] add_surface_patches!( geo, centers, normals, areas, p(x1, y2, z1), p(x2, y2, z1), p(x2, y1, z1), p(x1, y1, z1), (0.0, 0.0, -1.0) ) end # Top face if k == nz || !occupied[i, j, k+1] add_surface_patches!( geo, centers, normals, areas, p(x1, y1, z2), p(x2, y1, z2), p(x2, y2, z2), p(x1, y2, z2), (0.0, 0.0, 1.0) ) end end return ( mesh=build_mesh(geo), centers=centers, normals=normals, areas=areas, volume=partition.volume ) end # Extract architectural edges from the CSG boundary function generate_architectural_edges(design) partition = csg_partition(design) xs = partition.xs ys = partition.ys zs = partition.zs occupied = partition.occupied nx, ny, nz = size(occupied) # Store unique geometric edges edge_set = Set{ Tuple{NTuple{3,Float64},NTuple{3,Float64}} }() # Register each edge only once function add_edge!(a, b) p1 = ( Float64(a[1]), Float64(a[2]), Float64(a[3]) ) p2 = ( Float64(b[1]), Float64(b[2]), Float64(b[3]) ) if p1 == p2 return nothing end edge = isless(p1, p2) ? (p1, p2) : (p2, p1) push!(edge_set, edge) return nothing end # Register the four boundary edges of a face function add_face_edges!(a, b, c, d) add_edge!(a, b) add_edge!(b, c) add_edge!(c, d) add_edge!(d, a) return nothing end # Process every occupied CSG cell for i in 1:nx, j in 1:ny, k in 1:nz if !occupied[i, j, k] continue end x1, x2 = xs[i], xs[i+1] y1, y2 = ys[j], ys[j+1] z1, z2 = zs[k], zs[k+1] p(x, y, z) = (x, y, z) # Negative X boundary if i == 1 || !occupied[i-1, j, k] add_face_edges!( p(x1, y1, z1), p(x1, y1, z2), p(x1, y2, z2), p(x1, y2, z1) ) end # Positive X boundary if i == nx || !occupied[i+1, j, k] add_face_edges!( p(x2, y1, z1), p(x2, y2, z1), p(x2, y2, z2), p(x2, y1, z2) ) end # Negative Y boundary if j == 1 || !occupied[i, j-1, k] add_face_edges!( p(x1, y1, z1), p(x2, y1, z1), p(x2, y1, z2), p(x1, y1, z2) ) end # Positive Y boundary if j == ny || !occupied[i, j+1, k] add_face_edges!( p(x2, y2, z1), p(x1, y2, z1), p(x1, y2, z2), p(x2, y2, z2) ) end # Bottom boundary if k == 1 || !occupied[i, j, k-1] add_face_edges!( p(x1, y2, z1), p(x2, y2, z1), p(x2, y1, z1), p(x1, y1, z1) ) end # Top boundary if k == nz || !occupied[i, j, k+1] add_face_edges!( p(x1, y1, z2), p(x2, y1, z2), p(x2, y2, z2), p(x1, y2, z2) ) end end # Convert unique edges into line segments segments = Point3f[] for (a, b) in edge_set push!(segments, Point3f(a...)) push!(segments, Point3f(b...)) end return segments end # Calculate approximate solar position function solar_position(datetime) day_number = dayofyear(datetime) year_length = isleapyear(year(datetime)) ? 366 : 365 local_hour = Dates.hour(datetime) + Dates.minute(datetime) / 60 gamma = 2π / year_length * ( day_number - 1 + (local_hour - 12) / 24 ) equation_of_time = 229.18 * ( 0.000075 + 0.001868 * cos(gamma) - 0.032077 * sin(gamma) - 0.014615 * cos(2 * gamma) - 0.040849 * sin(2 * gamma) ) declination = 0.006918 - 0.399912 * cos(gamma) + 0.070257 * sin(gamma) - 0.006758 * cos(2 * gamma) + 0.000907 * sin(2 * gamma) - 0.002697 * cos(3 * gamma) + 0.00148 * sin(3 * gamma) solar_minutes = local_hour * 60 + equation_of_time + 4 * LONGITUDE - 60 * UTC_OFFSET hour_angle = deg2rad( solar_minutes / 4 - 180 ) lat = deg2rad(LATITUDE) sin_elevation = sin(lat) * sin(declination) + cos(lat) * cos(declination) * cos(hour_angle) elevation = rad2deg( asin(clamp(sin_elevation, -1.0, 1.0)) ) azimuth = mod( rad2deg( atan( sin(hour_angle), cos(hour_angle) * sin(lat) - tan(declination) * cos(lat) ) ) + 180, 360 ) return azimuth, elevation end # Convert solar angles to ENU coordinates # X = East, Y = North, Z = Up function sun_vector(azimuth, elevation) az = deg2rad(azimuth) el = deg2rad(elevation) return ( cos(el) * sin(az), cos(el) * cos(az), sin(el) ) end # Calculate ray intersection with a box function ray_box_interval(origin, direction, box) lower = (box.xmin, box.ymin, box.zmin) upper = (box.xmax, box.ymax, box.zmax) tmin = 0.0 tmax = Inf for axis in 1:3 o = origin[axis] d = direction[axis] if abs(d) < 1.0e-10 if o < lower[axis] || o > upper[axis] return nothing end else t1 = (lower[axis] - o) / d t2 = (upper[axis] - o) / d tmin = max(tmin, min(t1, t2)) tmax = min(tmax, max(t1, t2)) if tmax <= tmin return nothing end end end return (tmin, tmax) end # Test whether a solar ray is blocked by the CSG solid function ray_blocked(origin, direction, design) events = Float64[0.0] has_addition = false # Collect additive volume intersections for box in design.additions hit = ray_box_interval( origin, direction, box ) if hit !== nothing has_addition = true push!( events, hit[1], hit[2] ) end end if !has_addition return false end # Include subtraction boundaries for box in design.cutters hit = ray_box_interval( origin, direction, box ) if hit !== nothing push!( events, hit[1], hit[2] ) end end sort!(events) unique!(events) # Test every interval between successive events for i in 1:(length(events)-1) t1 = events[i] t2 = events[i+1] if t2 - t1 <= 1.0e-7 continue end t = (t1 + t2) / 2 x = origin[1] + direction[1] * t y = origin[2] + direction[2] * t z = origin[3] + direction[3] * t if inside_solid( x, y, z, design.additions, design.cutters ) return true end end return false end # Check direct sunlight on a ground point function ground_receives_sun(x, y, direction, design) if direction[3] <= 0.0 return false end origin = (x, y, 0.08) return !ray_blocked( origin, direction, design ) end # Check direct sunlight on a building surface function surface_receives_sun( center, normal, direction, design ) if direction[3] <= 0.0 return false end incidence = normal[1] * direction[1] + normal[2] * direction[2] + normal[3] * direction[3] if incidence <= 1.0e-6 return false end origin = ( center[1] + normal[1] * 0.08, center[2] + normal[2] * 0.08, center[3] + normal[3] * 0.08 ) return !ray_blocked( origin, direction, design ) end # Generate the analytical ground mesh function generate_ground_grid() geo = new_geometry() centers = NTuple{2,Float64}[] step = GROUND_STEP for x in GROUND_MIN:step:(GROUND_MAX-step) for y in GROUND_MIN:step:(GROUND_MAX-step) push!( centers, (x + step / 2, y + step / 2) ) add_quad!( geo, Point3f(x, y, -0.15), Point3f(x + step, y, -0.15), Point3f(x + step, y + step, -0.15), Point3f(x, y + step, -0.15) ) end end return ( mesh=build_mesh(geo), centers=centers ) end # Generate sun directions at fixed time intervals function daily_sun_vectors(date) vectors = NTuple{3,Float64}[] start_minutes = SUN_START_HOUR * 60 end_minutes = SUN_END_HOUR * 60 time_range = range( start_minutes, stop=end_minutes - SUN_INTERVAL, step=SUN_INTERVAL ) for minutes in time_range midpoint = minutes + SUN_INTERVAL ÷ 2 datetime = DateTime(date) + Minute(midpoint) azimuth, elevation = solar_position(datetime) if elevation > 0.0 push!( vectors, sun_vector(azimuth, elevation) ) end end return vectors end # Calculate direct sun hours on ground samples function calculate_ground_hours(design, date, centers) values = zeros(Float64, length(centers)) directions = daily_sun_vectors(date) dt = SUN_INTERVAL / 60 for (i, center) in enumerate(centers) x, y = center # Mark building footprints as invalid analysis cells if inside_solid( x, y, 0.05, design.additions, design.cutters ) values[i] = NaN continue end for direction in directions if ground_receives_sun( x, y, direction, design ) values[i] += dt end end end return values end # Calculate direct sun hours on building surfaces function calculate_surface_hours(design, date, surfaces) values = zeros( Float64, length(surfaces.centers) ) directions = daily_sun_vectors(date) dt = SUN_INTERVAL / 60 for i in eachindex(surfaces.centers) center = surfaces.centers[i] normal = surfaces.normals[i] # Exclude downward-facing building surfaces if normal[3] < -0.5 values[i] = NaN continue end for direction in directions if surface_receives_sun( center, normal, direction, design ) values[i] += dt end end end return values end # Convert sun hours into a heatmap color function heatmap_color(hours) if !isfinite(hours) return NEUTRAL_GROUND end t = Float32(clamp( hours / MAX_SUN_HOURS, 0.0, 1.0 )) position = t * 4f0 index = clamp( floor(Int, position) + 1, 1, 4 ) fraction = clamp( position - Float32(index - 1), 0f0, 1f0 ) a = SOLAR_PALETTE[index] b = SOLAR_PALETTE[index+1] return RGBf( (1f0 - fraction) * a.r + fraction * b.r, (1f0 - fraction) * a.g + fraction * b.g, (1f0 - fraction) * a.b + fraction * b.b ) end # Expand each analytical color to four vertices function expand_colors(cell_colors) result = RGBf[] sizehint!( result, 4 * length(cell_colors) ) for color in cell_colors append!( result, (color, color, color, color) ) end return result end # Calculate instantaneous ground shadow colors function shadow_ground_colors( design, centers, azimuth, elevation ) direction = sun_vector(azimuth, elevation) colors = RGBf[] for (x, y) in centers exposed = ground_receives_sun( x, y, direction, design ) push!( colors, exposed ? SUNLIT_COLOR : SHADOW_COLOR ) end return colors end # Calculate courtyard daily solar statistics function courtyard_statistics(design, date) courtyard = design.courtyard directions = daily_sun_vectors(date) values = Float64[] dt = SUN_INTERVAL / 60 for x in range( courtyard.xmin + 1, courtyard.xmax - 1, length=9 ) for y in range( courtyard.ymin + 1, courtyard.ymax - 1, length=9 ) if inside_solid( x, y, 0.05, design.additions, design.cutters ) continue end hours = 0.0 for direction in directions if ground_receives_sun( x, y, direction, design ) hours += dt end end push!(values, hours) end end if isempty(values) return ( average=0.0, minimum=0.0, maximum=0.0, shaded_percent=0.0 ) end return ( average=mean(values), minimum=minimum(values), maximum=maximum(values), shaded_percent= 100 * count(h -> h < 3.0, values) / length(values) ) end # Calculate area-weighted building solar statistics function surface_statistics(surfaces, hours) valid = [ i for i in eachindex(hours) if isfinite(hours[i]) && surfaces.normals[i][3] > -0.5 ] if isempty(valid) return ( average=0.0, minimum=0.0, maximum=0.0, shaded_percent=0.0 ) end total_area = sum( surfaces.areas[i] for i in valid ) average = sum( hours[i] * surfaces.areas[i] for i in valid ) / max(total_area, 1.0e-9) shaded_area = sum( surfaces.areas[i] for i in valid if hours[i] < 3.0 ) return ( average=average, minimum=minimum(hours[i] for i in valid), maximum=maximum(hours[i] for i in valid), shaded_percent= 100 * shaded_area / total_area ) end # Calculate the preliminary massing quality index function evaluate_design(design, surfaces, courtyard_stats) original_design = ( additions=design.additions, cutters=BoxVolume[] ) original_volume = csg_partition(original_design).volume void_ratio = clamp( 1 - surfaces.volume / max(original_volume, 1.0), 0.0, 1.0 ) volumes = [ (b.xmax - b.xmin) * (b.ymax - b.ymin) * (b.zmax - b.zmin) for b in design.additions ] dominance = maximum(volumes) / sum(volumes) void_score = 100 * clamp( 1 - abs(void_ratio - 0.25) / 0.25, 0.0, 1.0 ) dominance_score = 100 * clamp( 1 - abs(dominance - 0.50) / 0.50, 0.0, 1.0 ) sun_score = 100 * clamp( 1 - abs(courtyard_stats.average - 5.0) / 5.0, 0.0, 1.0 ) score = 0.35 * void_score + 0.30 * dominance_score + 0.35 * sun_score return ( score=score, void_ratio=void_ratio, dominance=dominance, volume=surfaces.volume ) end # Apply the initial camera framing fit_building!( initial_design; mode=:massing ) # Initialize the solar simulation update_solar_time!() # Display the complete architectural application display(fig) How the Solar Heatmap Guides Architectural Design While the Julia script does not run an automated optimization loop, the relationship between the Boolean massing and the solar simulation goes far beyond a passive scorecard at the end. In an interactive, human-in-the-loop workflow, the solar heatmap directly informs two layers of architectural decision-making:
Balancing Void Carving & Tropical Self-Shading: Every time a subtractive box (C₁–C₅) carves a courtyard or light slot into the monolith, it invites daylight deeper into the building core—while the taller tower (B₂) and cantilevered gallery (B₃) act as giant sunshades that block harsh equatorial radiation. In the selected Seed 2026 (Light Canyon) configuration, this geometric interplay shields 37.1% of the building’s surfaces under 3 hours of direct sun and keeps the central courtyard at a comfortable average of 1.11 sun hours/day. The Heatmap as a Material & Glazing Blueprint: Comparing the Combined Sun-Hours Heatmap with the final architectural design reveals how the simulation guides material placement: High-Exposure Orange & Red Zones (10.5 to 14 Hours): Across the roof planes and upper western facades where tropical solar radiation is most intense, the building responds with thick, windowless travertine and concrete thermal mass, cascading parapet greenery to absorb heat on the upper ledges, and timber shading louvers across the mouth of the vertical light slot (C₄). Self-Shaded Deep-Blue Zones (0 to 3.5 Hours): Inside the recessed entrance portal (C₂), the lower courtyard walls (C₁), and the lateral recess (C₅)—where the heatmap proves the facades are protected by the building’s own shadow throughout the day—the architect can confidently open up floor-to-ceiling glass walls for the reading library and semi-outdoor public lounge without risk of glare or overheating. From CSG Partition Grid to Physical Study Model Because the CSG algorithm partitions the building along the exact planes where the additive boxes (B₁–B₃) and subtractive cutters (C₁–C₅) intersect, it naturally generates a rhythmic grid of horizontal and vertical seam lines across the facade.
In the physical study model above—crafted from basswood blocks and museum board—these computational CSG partition lines become the tectonic joint pattern of the stone and concrete cladding, while the Boolean cutouts become a trellised roof skylight (C₄), a deeply shaded entrance portal (C₂), and a tranquil reflecting pool along the street edge.
Interior Daylight & Evening Presence Stepping inside the building reveals the spatial purpose of the Boolean subtractions:
The Vertical Light Slot & Central Courtyard: High overhead, the narrow light slot (C₄) and central courtyard (C₁) slice through the heavy travertine-and-concrete mass, channeling controlled beams of tropical daylight down into the double-height public lounge and glass-enclosed reading library while keeping the lower spaces cool and shaded (37.1% of building surfaces receive under 3 hours of direct sun). Tactile Warmth: Slatted timber ceilings, indoor tropical planting, and travertine benches soften the orthogonal geometry and connect the interior visually to the exterior reflecting basin. At night, the CSG partition lines that divided the computational mesh are reimagined as recessed linear lighting channels—tracing warm horizontal and vertical ribbons of light across the stone monolith while the carved entrance portal glows welcomingly along the avenue.

Concept & Climate-Informed Monoliths

Light-Sculpted Mass bridges generative form-finding and environmental performance analysis within a single interactive Julia application. Calibrated to the equatorial solar geometry of Bandung, Indonesia (6.9175° S, 107.6191° E), the project investigates how monumental, monolithic architecture can be carved open by courtyards, deep entrance portals, roof terraces, and narrow vertical light slots—and how those spatial voids perform under tropical daylight.

Rather than treating massing generation and solar simulation as separate stages across different software packages, this custom tool integrates Constructive Solid Geometry (CSG) directly with an analytical solar ray-casting engine and a real-time evaluation dashboard.

Concept & Spatial Tectonics Rather than manually sculpting static forms, Crystalline Monolith Pavilion investigates a rule-based approach to deconstructivist architecture. Set beside a tranquil reflecting pool within an urban park, the project explores the spatial tension between monolithic opaque volumes and faceted glass voids—testing how fractured geometric wedges can anchor firmly to the ground plane while projecting dramatic cantilevers over the water’s edge.
The resulting pavilion forms a luminous civic volume where massive white architectural concrete wedges collide and interlock, pierced by cyan-tinted structural glass fissures that filter daylight through a triangulated steel mullion framework.
The Computational Logic: Rule-Based Wedges The entire form is generated by a standalone Python script in Blender. As shown in the workflow diagram below, the script builds the pavilion through six clear steps:
Scene & Material Setup: Clears the 3D scene and creates four distinct architectural materials: smooth solid concrete, cyan-tinted transparent glass, dark steel mullion frames, and the plaza floor plane. Generating Angular Wedges: For each block, the script scatters 5 to 7 pairs of points in a ring and wraps them in a tight outer skin (convex hull)—creating a sharp, multi-faceted wedge without any self-intersecting surfaces. Slicing a Flat Base (Z = 0.02): After tilting and rotating each wedge in 3D space, the script slices off everything below ground level along a flat horizontal plane. This ensures that every cantilevered mass sits firmly on a flat structural footprint. Interlocking Concrete Solids & Glass Frames: Finally, the script spawns 6 to 8 solid concrete wedges interlocked with 3 to 4 glass volumes. Each glass volume is automatically duplicated and converted into a 12 cm thick wireframe cage to form its structural steel mullions. View Python Source Code (crystalline_monolith.py)import bpy import bmesh import random import math from mathutils import Vector, Euler # Clear existing scene objects and unused geometry data def clear_all(): # Remove all scene objects except the camera for obj in bpy.context.scene.objects: if obj.type != 'CAMERA': bpy.data.objects.remove(obj, do_unlink=True) # Remove existing mesh, material, and light datablocks for b in (bpy.data.meshes, bpy.data.materials, bpy.data.lights): for item in b: b.remove(item) # Configure the ambient world environment def setup_scene_ambient(): # Create a world environment if one does not already exist world = bpy.context.scene.world or bpy.data.worlds.new("World") bpy.context.scene.world = world world.use_nodes = True # Set the background color and ambient illumination strength bg = world.node_tree.nodes.get("Background") if bg: bg.inputs['Color'].default_value = (0.05, 0.06, 0.08, 1.0) bg.inputs['Strength'].default_value = 1.0 # Create and configure the materials used in the architectural composition def get_materials(): # Define the primary solid architectural material mat_solid = bpy.data.materials.new("Mat_Decon_Solid") mat_solid.use_nodes = True bsdf_s = mat_solid.node_tree.nodes.get("Principled BSDF") if bsdf_s: bsdf_s.inputs['Base Color'].default_value = (0.22, 0.24, 0.28, 1.0) bsdf_s.inputs['Roughness'].default_value = 0.18 # Configure specular reflection based on Blender shader version if 'Specular IOR Level' in bsdf_s.inputs: bsdf_s.inputs['Specular IOR Level'].default_value = 0.7 elif 'Specular' in bsdf_s.inputs: bsdf_s.inputs['Specular'].default_value = 0.7 # Create a transparent glass material using the Glass BSDF shader mat_glass = bpy.data.materials.new("Mat_Decon_Glass") mat_glass.use_nodes = True nodes_g = mat_glass.node_tree.nodes links_g = mat_glass.node_tree.links # Remove default shader nodes before creating the glass shader network nodes_g.clear() # Create the material output and glass shader nodes out_g = nodes_g.new('ShaderNodeOutputMaterial') bsdf_g = nodes_g.new('ShaderNodeBsdfGlass') # Define glass color, surface roughness, and refractive index bsdf_g.inputs['Color'].default_value = (0.6, 0.85, 0.98, 1.0) bsdf_g.inputs['Roughness'].default_value = 0.02 bsdf_g.inputs['IOR'].default_value = 1.52 # Connect the glass shader to the material surface output links_g.new(bsdf_g.outputs['BSDF'], out_g.inputs['Surface']) # Define the dark structural material for the glass mullion system mat_mullion = bpy.data.materials.new("Mat_Mullion") mat_mullion.use_nodes = True bsdf_m = mat_mullion.node_tree.nodes.get("Principled BSDF") if bsdf_m: bsdf_m.inputs['Base Color'].default_value = (0.05, 0.05, 0.06, 1.0) bsdf_m.inputs['Roughness'].default_value = 0.25 # Define the material for the surrounding ground plane mat_ground = bpy.data.materials.new("Mat_Plaza") mat_ground.use_nodes = True bsdf_gr = mat_ground.node_tree.nodes.get("Principled BSDF") if bsdf_gr: bsdf_gr.inputs['Base Color'].default_value = (0.06, 0.07, 0.09, 1.0) bsdf_gr.inputs['Roughness'].default_value = 0.5 # Return all four materials for use in the architectural scene return mat_solid, mat_glass, mat_mullion, mat_ground # Generate an irregular polyhedral wedge through procedural geometry def create_polyhedral_wedge(center, scale_vec, rot_euler): # Initialize an empty BMesh structure for direct mesh manipulation bm = bmesh.new() # Randomly determine the number of radial vertex pairs num_pts = random.randint(5, 7) # Define the initial radial dimension of the polyhedral geometry base_r = scale_vec.x # Generate randomly distributed angular positions around the center angles = sorted([random.uniform(0, 2 * math.pi) for _ in range(num_pts)]) # Define a displaced upper region to create an irregular wedge profile top_offset = Vector(( random.uniform(-scale_vec.x * 0.5, scale_vec.x * 0.5), random.uniform(-scale_vec.y * 0.5, scale_vec.y * 0.5), scale_vec.z )) # Generate alternating lower and upper vertices for a in angles: # Introduce radial variation to avoid regular geometric patterns r = base_r * random.uniform(0.7, 1.3) # Calculate the lower vertex coordinates bx = math.cos(a) * r by = math.sin(a) * r * (scale_vec.y / scale_vec.x) # Create the lower vertex of the polyhedral structure bm.verts.new(Vector((bx, by, -scale_vec.z * 0.2))) # Calculate the upper vertex with additional positional variation tx = bx * random.uniform(0.4, 1.2) + top_offset.x ty = by * random.uniform(0.4, 1.2) + top_offset.y tz = top_offset.z + random.uniform(-scale_vec.z * 0.15, scale_vec.z * 0.15) # Create the upper vertex of the polyhedral structure bm.verts.new(Vector((tx, ty, tz))) # Construct a convex hull from the generated vertices # This creates an irregular solid volume without predefined geometry bmesh.ops.convex_hull(bm, input=bm.verts) # Convert the specified Euler rotation into a transformation matrix rmat = rot_euler.to_matrix().to_4x4() # Apply the object's spatial translation rmat.translation = center # Transform the entire polyhedral geometry using rotation and translation bmesh.ops.transform(bm, matrix=rmat, verts=bm.verts) # Apply a horizontal planar bisect operation at Z = 0.02 # This removes geometry on one side of the cutting plane bmesh.ops.bisect_plane( bm, geom=bm.verts[:] + bm.edges[:] + bm.faces[:], plane_co=(0, 0, 0.02), plane_no=(0, 0, 1), clear_inner=True ) # Update vertex indexing and recalculate surface normals bm.verts.ensure_lookup_table() bm.normal_update() # Return the completed procedural geometry return bm # Assemble the complete deconstructivist architectural composition def build_pure_deconstructivism_scene(): # Reset the scene and initialize its environment clear_all() setup_scene_ambient() # Retrieve all architectural materials mat_solid, mat_glass, mat_mullion, mat_ground = get_materials() # Generate a randomized collection of solid architectural volumes num_solids = random.randint(6, 8) for i in range(num_solids): # Randomize the spatial position of each solid volume center = Vector(( random.uniform(-9.0, 9.0), random.uniform(-9.0, 9.0), random.uniform(4.0, 11.0) )) # Randomize the proportions of each architectural volume scale_vec = Vector(( random.uniform(14.0, 22.0), random.uniform(7.0, 12.0), random.uniform(6.0, 10.0) )) # Apply random three-dimensional rotations rot_euler = Euler(( math.radians(random.uniform(-22, 22)), math.radians(random.uniform(-22, 22)), math.radians(random.uniform(0, 360)) ), 'XYZ') # Generate the irregular polyhedral geometry bm_s = create_polyhedral_wedge(center, scale_vec, rot_euler) # Convert BMesh geometry into a Blender mesh datablock mesh_s = bpy.data.meshes.new(f"Solid_Mesh_{i+1}") bm_s.to_mesh(mesh_s) bm_s.free() # Create the architectural solid object and link it to the scene obj_s = bpy.data.objects.new(f"Solid_Block_{i+1}", mesh_s) bpy.context.collection.objects.link(obj_s) # Assign the primary solid material obj_s.data.materials.append(mat_solid) # Generate a separate collection of transparent glass volumes num_glass_volumes = random.randint(3, 4) for j in range(num_glass_volumes): # Randomize the position of each glass volume g_center = Vector(( random.uniform(-5.0, 6.0), random.uniform(-5.0, 6.0), random.uniform(4.0, 9.0) )) # Define randomized dimensions for the glass structures g_scale = Vector(( random.uniform(10.0, 16.0), random.uniform(8.0, 14.0), random.uniform(8.0, 15.0) )) # Introduce independent rotational variations g_rot = Euler(( math.radians(random.uniform(-25, 25)), math.radians(random.uniform(-25, 25)), math.radians(random.uniform(0, 360)) ), 'XYZ') # Generate the procedural glass geometry bm_g = create_polyhedral_wedge(g_center, g_scale, g_rot) # Convert the generated geometry into a Blender mesh mesh_g = bpy.data.meshes.new(f"Glass_Mesh_{j+1}") bm_g.to_mesh(mesh_g) bm_g.free() # Create the transparent architectural glass object obj_glass = bpy.data.objects.new(f"Glass_Structure_{j+1}", mesh_g) bpy.context.collection.objects.link(obj_glass) # Assign the transparent glass material obj_glass.data.materials.append(mat_glass) # Duplicate the glass object to generate its structural frame obj_frame = obj_glass.copy() obj_frame.data = obj_glass.data.copy() obj_frame.name = f"Glass_Mullions_{j+1}" bpy.context.collection.objects.link(obj_frame) # Replace the glass material with the dark mullion material obj_frame.data.materials.clear() obj_frame.data.materials.append(mat_mullion) # Apply a Wireframe modifier to generate the structural framework mod_wf = obj_frame.modifiers.new("Mullion_Wireframe", 'WIREFRAME') # Define the thickness of the mullion elements mod_wf.thickness = 0.12 # Replace the original surface with the wireframe geometry mod_wf.use_replace = True # Create the ground plane using BMesh bm_p = bmesh.new() # Generate a large planar grid to represent the surrounding plaza bmesh.ops.create_grid(bm_p, x_segments=1, y_segments=1, size=300.0) # Convert the ground geometry into a Blender mesh mesh_p = bpy.data.meshes.new("Plaza_Mesh") bm_p.to_mesh(mesh_p) bm_p.free() # Create the plaza object and link it to the scene plaza = bpy.data.objects.new("Plaza_Ground", mesh_p) bpy.context.collection.objects.link(plaza) # Assign the ground material plaza.data.materials.append(mat_ground) # Deselect all objects to leave the scene in a neutral state bpy.ops.object.select_all(action='DESELECT') # Execute the procedural architectural generation build_pure_deconstructivism_scene() From Digital Hulls to Physical Study Model Because the script wraps each volume in flat polygonal faces and slices the bottom cleanly along a horizontal plane, the entire building avoids complex double-curved surfaces.
As shown in the physical study model above, these geometric wedges translate directly into flat white concrete panels and straight steel-and-acrylic glazing frames sitting over a recessed reflecting pool—proving that dramatic deconstructivist forms can be built from flat formwork and straight steel profiles.
Interior Space & Evening Reflection Inside the pavilion, the collision between solid concrete wedges and glazed volumes creates a bright, double-height exhibition hall:
Tilted Concrete Walls & Mezzanine: Sloped white concrete walls—washed by warm hidden cove lighting along the ceiling folds—guide visitors up a central stair to a cantilevered mezzanine walkway. Triangulated Glass & Park Views: Along the water’s edge, the faceted cyan-blue glass wall opens the lounge and gallery to views of the reflecting pool and city park, while its triangulated steel frame casts crisp geometric shadows across the floor. While the Python script only calculates geometric wedges and flat ground cuts, the architectural setting creates a striking contrast between heavy concrete mass and quiet reflection. Placing the cantilevered wedges beside a still water basin lets the pool mirror the geometry and soften its sharp angles. At twilight, exterior uplights graze the white concrete folds while warm gallery light glows outward through the glass fissures across the dark water.
summary:
Concept & Spatial Tectonics

Rather than manually sculpting static forms, Crystalline Monolith Pavilion investigates a rule-based approach to deconstructivist architecture. Set beside a tranquil reflecting pool within an urban park, the project explores the spatial tension between monolithic opaque volumes and faceted glass voids—testing how fractured geometric wedges can anchor firmly to the ground plane while projecting dramatic cantilevers over the water’s edge.

The resulting pavilion forms a luminous civic volume where massive white architectural concrete wedges collide and interlock, pierced by cyan-tinted structural glass fissures that filter daylight through a triangulated steel mullion framework.
title: Crystalline Monolith Pavilion

For hundreds of years, an architect was a maker. To design meant to touch materials: pencil on paper, wood models on a desk, and slow, careful lines drawn by hand.
Today, an artificial intelligence can create 100 room layouts, building facades, and 3D shapes in ten seconds. Because the computer generates forms so fast, we face an existential question:
If the machine makes everything, what is the human for?
Many say the architect is now just a curator—someone who looks at images and picks the best one. But if curation only means clicking on pretty pictures, architecture loses its soul.
To survive, architecture must understand what craft really is: not just moving hands, but giving meaning to choices.
The Blind Machine: The “Selection Problem” A computer can beat a grandmaster at chess, but the computer does not know it is playing a game. It has no feelings, no memories, and no idea what warmth or sunlight feels like.
When an AI generates 100 building plans, 99 of them might be structurally safe and look beautiful. But how do we decide which one is right?
This is the Selection Problem.
A machine can answer how to shape a wall. But only a human can answer why that wall belongs in this neighborhood, for these people, at this moment in history.
Choosing is not a shortcut; choosing is a heavy moral responsibility. If a building feels cold, lonely, or unsafe, the architect cannot blame the code. The architect must stand in front of the community and defend the choice.
The Extended Mind: Two Kinds of Curation Philosophers note that when a blind person walks with a white stick, the stick is no longer just wood—it becomes part of their body. The person “sees” through the stick.
Writer Neil Leach says AI is like this stick: it is an extended mind. AI is not an outside enemy taking our work; it is an extra layer of human thought.
Because of this, curating happens in two different ways:
Curating the Results: Looking at the 100 designs and judging them with human empathy and local context. Curating the Tools: Deciding how the computer thinks. Think of a painter choosing a fine brush versus a wide palette knife. The tool is not passive; the tool shapes the imagination before the first drop of paint hits the canvas.
When an architect chooses which AI model to run, they are designing the rules of thought. Choosing the tool is the first act of design.
The Rise of the “Meta-Designer” This transforms the craft:
The traditional maker focused on drawing the object. The careless user accepts whatever the algorithm spits out. The meta-designer designs the system, guides the questions, and checks the results with wisdom. Craft was never just about muscle memory in our fingers. Craft has always been about care, judgment, and purpose.
Beyond the Screen When paper was invented, people worried memory would die. When computers arrived in studios thirty years ago, people feared drawings would lose their heart.
Now, in an age where images cost nothing to make, the most valuable thing an architect owns is not drafting speed. It is the quiet wisdom to say: “The machine made 100 forms, but this is the only one that honors human life.”

Setiap kali menghadiri seminar atau pameran arsitektur digital di tanah air, narasi yang disuguhkan hampir selalu seragam: kurva percepatan proyek yang fantastis, visualisasi terintegrasi, serta janji manis efisiensi biaya lewat adopsi Building Information Modelling (BIM). Kita terbiasa merayakan angka, akurasi, dan deretan perangkat lunak mutakhir. Namun, ada satu panggung yang nyaris selalu luput disorot: bilik-bilik kerja studio arsitektur dan konsultan perencana di mana lampu monitor menyala hingga subuh, ditemani mata para desainer dan engineer yang kelelahan.
Digitalisasi konstruksi di Indonesia menyimpan paradoks yang getir. Alih-alih meringankan beban kerja dan menciptakan ruang kolaborasi yang sehat, kehadiran teknologi kerap kali hanya mengamplifikasi eksploitasi. Di atas kertas, koordinasi model berjalan mulus tanpa tabrakan (clash-free), tetapi di dunia nyata, benturan antara ekspektasi manajemen yang nir-empati dan batas fisik manusia kian tak terelakkan.
Kita terlalu sibuk memodernisasi alat kerja, namun lupa memperbarui kultur sosial yang menjalankannya. Jika efisiensi digital pada akhirnya hanya dibayar dengan hilangnya hak akhir pekan, kultur revisi tanpa henti, dan percepatan burnout, maka apa yang selama ini kita sebut sebagai “kemajuan” sesungguhnya hanyalah ilusi.
Panggung Seminar vs. Bilik Lembur: Menguak Ilusi Efisiensi Di atas panggung seminar, transformasi digital industri konstruksi tampak begitu berkilau. Slide presentasi berganti menampilkan kurva percepatan proyek yang tajam, koordinasi multidisiplin tanpa celah, hingga animasi model BIM yang berputar mulus memperlihatkan federasi struktur, arsitektur, dan MEP yang clash-free. Para pembicara dengan lantang membacakan metrik keberhasilan: reduksi waktu gambar kerja hingga 40%, efisiensi material, dan kemudahan kolaborasi berbasis cloud. Di ruangan ber-AC dingin itu, masa depan konstruksi Indonesia terasa sudah tiba.
Namun, jarak antara panggung seminar dan bilik kerja studio perancangan terbentang begitu jauh.
Tepat beberapa jam setelah tepuk tangan seminar mereda, di sudut-sudut kantor konsultan perencana dan kontraktor, kenyataan sesungguhnya berlangsung. Monitor kerja masih menyala terang melewati tengah malam. Di depannya, arsitek muda, BIM modeler, dan engineer menatap layar dengan mata merah, ditemani cangkir kopi ketiga dan tumpukan kotak makanan instan. Efisiensi 40% yang dipaparkan tadi siang tidak pernah mewujud menjadi waktu istirahat yang lebih manusiawi. Efisiensi itu justru langsung diserap habis oleh target deadline baru yang dipercepat secara tidak masuk akal.
Inilah ilusi terbesar digitalisasi konstruksi kita: kecepatan alat disalahartikan sebagai kapasitas manusia.
Ketika perangkat lunak mampu menghasilkan potongan, denah, dan jadwal material secara otomatis dalam hitungan detik, manajemen proyek kerap mengasumsikan bahwa proses berpikir, analisis teknis, dan koordinasi manusia di baliknya bisa dipangkas dengan rasio yang sama. Ada jurang pemisah yang lebar antara kemajuan komputasi dan kematangan kultur kerja:
Peralatan Melompat, Pola Pikir Tertinggal: Kita telah mengadopsi perangkat lunak abad ke-21, tetapi masih mengoperasikannya dengan mentalitas manajemen lapangan abad ke-19 yang memandang tenaga kerja perencana sebagai buruh manual pembuat gambar.
Redefinisi Efisiensi yang Salah Kaprah: Efisiensi tidak lagi diartikan sebagai “menyelesaikan pekerjaan berkualitas dalam jam kerja wajar”, melainkan “memeras output sebanyak mungkin dalam batas fisik manusia yang tersisa”.
Glorifikasi Lembur sebagai Standar: Lembur hingga subuh—yang seharusnya menjadi alarm merah atas kegagalan perencanaan dan manajemen proyek—justru dinormalisasi bahkan diglorifikasi sebagai bentuk ‘dedikasi’ dan ‘passion’.
Digitalisasi yang berjalan tanpa kesadaran sosial pada akhirnya tidak membebaskan perencana dari beban kerja mekanis; ia hanya mempercepat putaran roda eksploitasi. Selama panggung seminar hanya merayakan metrik teknis tanpa pernah menanyakan jam tidur para pelakunya, efisiensi digital di Indonesia akan tetap menjadi mitos yang dibayar mahal oleh kesehatan mental para praktisi.
Anatomi Kultur Sosial yang Toksik: Saat Teknologi Mempercepat Burnout Kecanggihan perangkat lunak tidak otomatis melahirkan lingkungan kerja yang beradab. Di banyak ekosistem proyek di Indonesia, digitalisasi justru menjadi akselerator burnout karena bertabrakan dengan kultur kerja yang sejak awal sudah timpang. Tanpa rambu-rambu etik dan batasan operasional yang jelas, fitur-fitur otomasi BIM kerap dimanfaatkan untuk melegitimasi pola kerja yang merusak.
Ada tiga pola destruktif yang paling sering menjerat para perencana di lapangan:
Mitos “Tinggal Klik” dan Revisi Tanpa Batas: Sebelum era BIM, klien dan manajemen proyek berpikir dua kali sebelum meminta perubahan layout besar karena sadar tim harus merevisi puluhan lembar gambar secara manual. Kini, logika tersebut terbalik. Pemahaman dangkal bahwa “BIM serba otomatis” melahirkan asumsi keliru bahwa memindahkan core tangga atau mengubah fasad gedung setinggi 30 lantai hanyalah perkara “menggeser kursor dan klik”. Revisi diminta berulang kali tanpa batasan siklus, tanpa adendum kontrak, dan tanpa tambahan waktu pengerjaan—mengabaikan efek domino parametrik terhadap struktur dan MEP yang tetap butuh kalkulasi matang.
Sindrom “Rapat Jumat Sore, Beres Senin Pagi”: Pola koordinasi klasik yang terus berulang adalah rapat koordinasi yang sengaja dijadwalkan pada hari Jumat pukul 16.00 WIB, ditutup dengan instruksi: “Perubahannya tolong diakomodasi dan model federasi terbarunya siap di-review Senin pagi jam 09.00.” Ini adalah bentuk pelemparan inkompetensi manajemen waktu. Ketidakmampuan stakeholder menyusun jadwal diterjemahkan menjadi perampasan hak istirahat akhir pekan para arsitek dan engineer, seolah hari Sabtu dan Minggu adalah jam kerja cadangan gratis bagi proyek.
Invasi Hari Minggu dan Erosi Batas Profesional: Grup komunikasi instan proyek telah menghancurkan batas antara ruang kerja dan ranah privat. Bukan hal aneh lagi bagi seorang perencana menerima pesan WhatsApp bernada mendesak dari pihak Manajemen Konstruksi (MK) atau kontraktor pada Minggu siang: “Pak/Bu, tolong kirim potongan detail area ramp basement sekarang, tim lapangan mau cor besok pagi.” Tidak ada basa-basi, tidak ada rasa bersalah, dan ketiadaan respons langsung di hari libur kerap dilabeli sebagai sikap “tidak kooperatif”.
Teknologi digital menjanjikan alur kerja yang rapi dan terukur. Namun, ketika diterapkan di atas kultur yang feodal dan nir-empati, kecanggihan itu hanya melahirkan alat baru untuk memperas kapasitas manusia hingga titik nadir.
Membaca Ulang Randy Deutsch: Mengapa BIM Bukan Sekadar Soal Software Kekacauan kultur kerja yang kita alami di tanah air sesungguhnya telah lama diprediksi oleh para pemikir desain integratif global. Salah satu yang paling lantang menyuarakan aspek ini adalah Randy Deutsch, arsitek dan pengajar asal Amerika Serikat yang banyak menulis tentang irisan antara teknologi, proses, dan perilaku manusia dalam arsitektur—terutama melalui karyanya seperti BIM and Integrated Design dan Superusers.
Gagasan utama Deutsch bertumpu pada satu premis fundamental: BIM pada dasarnya adalah masalah sosial, bukan masalah perangkat lunak.
Deutsch menegaskan bahwa adopsi teknologi secanggih apa pun akan gagal mencapai potensi transformatifnya jika dinamika relasi antarmanusia (human dynamics) tidak dibenahi terlebih dahulu. Teknologi hanyalah pengungkit (amplifier). Jika kultur kerja awal sudah eksploitatif, tertutup, dan saling menyalahkan, digitalisasi hanya akan mempercepat dan memperluas skala eksploitasi tersebut.
Dalam konteks industri konstruksi kita, kegagalan terbesar adopsi BIM terjadi karena kita mengabaikan prinsip-prinsip relasional yang digariskan Deutsch:
Miskonsepsi Kolaborasi vs. Sekadar Koordinasi File: Industri kita kerap mengira bahwa menaruh model 3D di Common Data Environment (CDE) atau menggabungkan file arsitektur-struktur di software federasi sudah berarti “berkolaborasi”. Padahal, kolaborasi sejati menurut Deutsch menuntut trust, transparansi data sejak tahap awal, dan kerendahan hati untuk saling berbagi risiko. Yang terjadi di lapangan sering kali hanya koordinasi teknis file di permukaan, sementara mentalitas masing-masing disiplin tetap tersekat (siloed) dan saling melempar tanggung jawab saat muncul revisi.
Mengorbankan “Social Capital” demi “Digital Assets”: Manajemen proyek di Indonesia terlalu terobsesi mengejar kematangan aset digital—seperti akurasi Level of Development (LOD) atau clash-free report—namun abai membangun social capital. Deutsch mengingatkan bahwa keberhasilan proyek kompleks bergantung pada empati timbal balik: memahami beban kerja disiplin lain, menghargai waktu analisis desainer, dan membangun komunikasi psikologis yang aman tanpa intimidasi hierarkis.
Peran Superuser yang Tereduksi Menjadi Sekadar Operator: Alih-alih memposisikan arsitek dan BIM modeler sebagai knowledge workers atau superusers yang menjembatani inovasi desain dengan efisiensi konstruksi, sistem kita mereduksi mereka menjadi sekadar juru gambar cepat berkecepatan tinggi (fast-paced draftsperson) yang wajib tunduk pada instruksi sepihak.
Membaca ulang gagasan Randy Deutsch memberi kita cermin telak: digitalisasi konstruksi di Indonesia tersendat bukan karena para arsitek dan insinyurnya kurang piawai mengoperasikan software, melainkan karena ekosistem kita menolak mendewasakan kultur sosial yang menaunginya.
Menggagas Human-Centric BIM: Menaruh Manusia di Pusat Alur Kerja Berangkat dari kritik Randy Deutsch dan keprihatinan atas realitas lapangan, industri konstruksi Indonesia membutuhkan reposisi paradigma yang fundamental: Human-Centric BIM.
Konsep ini lahir dari kesadaran sederhana bahwa secanggih apa pun algoritma komputasi, model parametrik, atau platform cloud, jantung dari setiap garis yang ditarik dan setiap elemen yang dimodelkan adalah manusia. Human-Centric BIM menolak gagasan bahwa keberhasilan adopsi teknologi hanya diukur dari metrik mekanis seperti capaian LOD, volume gambar yang diproduksi per hari, atau kecepatan rendering.
Sebaliknya, pendekatan ini menetapkan parameter baru: sejauh mana implementasi teknologi mampu menjaga martabat, kesehatan mental, dan kapasitas intelektual para perancang dan insinyur.
Penerapan Human-Centric BIM bertumpu pada tiga pilar operasional:
Desain Alur Kerja Berbasis Kapasitas Manusiawi (Humane Workload Management): Menghentikan kalkulasi timeline proyek yang berbasis pada “kecepatan render komputer” dan menggantinya dengan estimasi realistis berbasis “waktu berpikir dan analisis manusia”. Mengakomodasi buffer time untuk koordinasi lintas disiplin tanpa harus memotong jam istirahat atau akhir pekan tim perencana.
Transparansi Risiko dan Kejelasan Batasan Perubahan (Scope Boundary Protocol): Menggunakan model digital bukan sebagai kanvas revisi instan tanpa batas, melainkan sebagai alat verifikasi keputusan sejak awal. Setiap iterasi desain harus memiliki matriks dampak yang jelas: jika geometri utama berubah, ada konsekuensi rasional terhadap waktu, biaya, dan beban kerja disiplin terkait yang disepakati bersama secara transparan oleh owner, MK, dan konsultan.
Rehabilitasi Posisi Arsitek dan Modeler sebagai Inovator, Bukan Operator: Mengembalikan fungsi esensial perancang sebagai pemecah masalah spasial dan tektonik. Otomasi dan komputasi parametrik harus difungsikan untuk memangkas tugas-tugas repetitif yang melelahkan (drudgery), sehingga waktu yang tersisa dapat dialokasikan untuk eksplorasi desain yang lebih berkualitas dan mendalam, bukan untuk menambal kesalahan komunikasi manajemen.
Menjadikan BIM berpusat pada manusia bukan berarti memperlambat laju proyek atau menolak kemajuan teknologi. Justru sebaliknya, alur kerja yang menghargai kapasitas kognitif dan waktu istirahat perencana terbukti meminimalkan human error, menekan angka turnover talenta berbakat, dan menghasilkan koordinasi lapangan yang jauh lebih solid.
Rekonstruksi Ekosistem: Menata Ulang Batasan dan Etika Industri Mengurai benang kusut ini menuntut keberanian merombak tata kelola industri kita secara struktural. Kemudahan komputasi parametrik harus diimbangi dengan batas regulasi yang tegas, mulai dari pengetatan klausul kontrak terkait siklus revisi, penyesuaian fee yang proporsional, hingga moratorium komunikasi di luar jam kerja. Menormalisasi pesan instan proyek di hari libur atau menuntut hasil rapat Jumat sore selesai pada Senin pagi bukanlah bentuk loyalitas, melainkan cermin dari tata kelola proyek yang cacat dan nir-etika.
Pada akhirnya, sebuah karya arsitektur tidak hanya berdiri di atas beton dan baja, melainkan dari waktu hidup manusia yang terserap di balik meja perancangan.
Ketika kita terus memuja digitalisasi hanya dari kecepatan garis dan kurva percepatan proyek yang dipaksakan, kita sedang mereduksi profesi mulia ini menjadi sekadar pabrik komputasi tanpa jiwa. Kemajuan teknologi yang memakan kesehatan mental dan merampas martabat para pelakunya bukanlah sebuah lompatan peradaban, melainkan bentuk eksploitasi usang berselubung antarmuka modern. Digitalisasi konstruksi di Indonesia tidak akan pernah mencapai kematangan sejatinya selama kita menolak memanusiakan mereka yang menjalankannya; sebab secanggih apa pun masa depan yang kita rancang, ia tak akan pernah kokoh berdiri di atas fondasi manusia-manusia yang remuk.
summary: Setiap kali menghadiri seminar atau pameran arsitektur digital di tanah air, narasi yang disuguhkan hampir selalu seragam: kurva percepatan proyek yang fantastis, visualisasi terintegrasi, serta janji manis efisiensi biaya lewat adopsi Building Information Modelling (BIM). Kita terbiasa merayakan angka, akurasi, dan deretan perangkat lunak mutakhir. Namun, ada satu panggung yang nyaris selalu luput disorot: bilik-bilik kerja studio arsitektur dan konsultan perencana di mana lampu monitor menyala hingga subuh, ditemani mata para desainer dan engineer yang kelelahan.
title: Ilusi Efisiensi: Mengapa Digitalisasi Konstruksi di Indonesia Gagal Membenahi Kultur Sosial Kita?

Kekecewaan arsitek terhadap kecerdasan buatan (artificial intelligence) sering kali berpangkal pada kekeliruan ekspektasi: memperlakukan sistem generatif layaknya asisten manusia yang memiliki intuisi ruang, lalu memprotes hasilnya ketika bentukan yang lahir terasa janggal, tidak tektonis, atau melenceng dari intensi desain.
Protes semacam ini kerap lahir dari ketidaktahuan kita terhadap apa yang sesungguhnya terjadi di dalam “kotak hitam” (black box) tersebut. Sebagaimana ditegaskan Neil Leach, AI bukanlah entitas berpikiran sadar dan bukan pula sekadar perangkat lunak CAD berbasis geometri pasti. AI adalah mesin pengenalan pola probabilistik. Memprotes hasil keluarannya tanpa memahami epistemologi di balik cara ia belajar dan berpikir adalah sebuah kenaifan metodologis.
Untuk dapat berdialog secara kritis dan berdaya dengan teknologi ini, para perancang perlu memahami dua pilar fundamental yang membentuk logikanya: bagaimana sistem tersebut dilatih, serta aliran paradigma apa yang menggerakkan cara kerjanya.
Tiga Rezim Pembelajaran: Mengapa Mesin “Melihat” Berbeda dengan Arsitek Keluaran visual atau spasial dari AI adalah manifestasi langsung dari data latihnya. Mesin tidak memahami “arsitektur” sebagai pengalaman spasial, melainkan sebagai korelasi matematis melalui tiga pendekatan:
Pembelajaran Terarah (Supervised Learning): Model belajar dari jutaan pasangan data yang diberi label oleh manusia. Jika kita meminta AI merancang denah dan hasilnya menghasilkan ruang tanpa ventilasi, kegagalan tersebut bukan karena mesin “bodoh”, melainkan karena korpus data latihnya hanya memetakan relasi visual dua dimensi tanpa pemahaman relasional mengenai fisika bangunan atau sirkulasi udara.
Pembelajaran Tak Terarah (Unsupervised Learning): Algoritma mencari pola intrinsik dari data mentah tanpa arahan manusia, lalu membangun ruang laten (latent space) berdimensi tinggi. Bentukan asing atau hibrida tipologi yang sering diprotes arsitek sejatinya adalah navigasi mesin di dalam ruang laten tersebut—menggabungkan karakteristik morfologis berdasarkan kedekatan matematis, bukan aturan tektonika konvensional.
Pembelajaran Penguatan (Reinforcement Learning): Sistem bertindak layaknya agen yang bereksperimen di dalam lingkungan simulasi berbasis reward dan penalti. Kualitas keluarannya sepenuhnya bergantung pada bagaimana parameter optimasi dirumuskan. Jika formula tujuannya bias atau tidak lengkap, mesin akan menghasilkan geometri anomali yang secara matematis optimal, namun secara spasial tidak masuk akal.
Lima Aliran Epistemologis: Memahami Ragam Karakter Komputasi Ketidaksesuaian hasil sering kali terjadi karena arsitek menuntut penalaran logika deduktif dari sistem yang bekerja secara probabilistik. Meminjam sintesis Pedro Domingos yang dielaborasi Leach, komputasi AI terbagi ke dalam lima aliran pemikiran yang memiliki watak berbeda:
Aliran Simbolis (Symbolists): Berpijak pada logika formal dan aturan eksplisit (rule-based). Sangat presisi untuk fungsi-fungsi deterministik (seperti pengecekan regulasi zonasi atau modul struktur), tetapi kaku dan gagal menangani nuansa estetika atau ambiguitas konteks tapak.
Aliran Koneksionis (Connectionists): Mengandalkan jejaring saraf tiruan (artificial neural networks) dan menjadi motor utama AI generatif saat ini. Aliran ini sangat piawai menangkap gaya, tekstur, dan impresi visual melalui asosiasi data raksasa, namun secara inheren tidak memahami logika tektonika struktural yang kaku.
Aliran Evolusioner (Evolutionaries): Menggunakan algoritma genetika untuk menguji, memutasi, dan mengawinsilangkan variasi desain demi menemukan bentuk paling optimal. Pendekatan ini membutuhkan perumusan fungsi kebugaran (fitness function) yang ketat; tanpa batasan yang presisi, bentuk yang berevolusi akan kehilangan keterbangunannya.
Aliran Bayesian (Bayesians): Bekerja berdasarkan kalkulasi probabilitas dan pembaruan keyakinan data di tengah ketidakpastian. Pendekatan ini relevan untuk pemodelan iklim mikro atau analisis kepadatan sirkulasi, namun tidak menghasilkan bentuk visual secara langsung.
Aliran Analogis (Analogizers): Mengambil keputusan berdasarkan rekognisi kemiripan antar-kasus (case-based). Sistem memproyeksikan preseden lama ke masalah baru. Jika keluarannya terasa klise atau repetitif, itu karena korpus presedennya tidak cukup luas untuk memicu lompatan tipologis baru.
Dari Mengeluh Menjadi Mengkurasi: Literasi Sebelum Artikulasi Menolak AI karena “hasilnya tidak masuk akal” atau menelannya mentah-mentah sebagai “keajaiban otomatis” adalah dua sikap yang sama-sama keliru.
Arsitek tidak dapat menuntut sistem koneksionis untuk berpikir deduktif layaknya sistem simbolis, atau mengharapkan mesin generatif memahami tektonika material jika data latihnya hanya berupa representasi gambar piksel semata.
Pemahaman atas teknik pelatihan dan lima aliran ini menuntut redefinisi peran profesional kita: dari pembuat bentuk manual menjadi kurator sistemik dan arsitek data. Sebelum tergesa-gesa memprotes piksel yang melenceng atau geometri yang anomali, pahami terlebih dahulu epistemologi mesin yang sedang digunakan. Hanya dengan literasi komputasional yang mendalam, arsitek dapat mengarahkan ruang laten AI secara presisi, kritis, dan berdaya guna.

That was the feedback from our 3D artists. They had just received a SketchUp model that was exported from Revit—the standard workflow for our government building project. The geometry was a disaster: broken faces, missing materials, random layers, and no logical structure. Hours of cleanup work lay ahead. And this wasn’t the first time.
Every project, the same story. A Revit model needs to move to SketchUp for visualization, rendering, or further design development. And every time, the transfer damages the model so badly that it almost feels like starting over.
Why does this keep happening? The official solutions are limited.
We don’t have access to SketchUp Studio, which includes an official Revit importer. Even if we did, we’ve heard mixed reviews—some say it works, others say it still loses important data. That leaves us with the traditional fallbacks: export to DWG or IFC.
These formats are “standard,” but they’re not designed for a clean, data-rich transfer. Exporting to DWG often flattens the model, losing Revit’s intelligent categories and parameters. IFC, while better for data, can create an unmanageable number of components, each one treated as a unique object. The result? A SketchUp model that is heavy, messy, and stripped of the BIM information that makes the Revit model so valuable.
This wasn’t just an inconvenience; it was a failure of interoperability. We were losing the intelligence of our model in the translation.
So I decided to build my own bridge.
I created a custom workflow that uses JSON as a neutral data format. The process is simple:
A Revit Add-In exports selected geometry, materials, and BIM parameters into a JSON file. A SketchUp Extension reads that JSON and reconstructs the model, organizing elements by Revit category and preserving as much information as possible.
The goal was to transfer not just the shape, but the identity of the model—its categories, parameters, and logic.
But here’s the honest truth: I don’t yet know if this will be truly useful. BIM data in SketchUp is an experiment. Architects and modelers in SketchUp might not need or want all that information. Maybe the geometry is enough. Maybe the BIM parameters just add clutter.
I built this tool with a hope, not an answer. I hope that someday, I’ll understand if this approach actually improves workflows or if it’s simply a technical curiosity.
I know every stakeholder has different needs. Our 3D artist wants clean geometry and materials. A project manager wants to query data. A client wants to understand the design. Everyone interacts with the model differently.
What I truly want is a seamless, interoperable way for data to move between tools—without losing its meaning along the way. I want a model to remain intelligent, no matter which software opens it. This is a small step toward that vision.
So, I made it open source. I shared it for free on GitHub.
I don’t know if it will be widely adopted. I don’t know if the BIM data in SketchUp will prove valuable or just be ignored. But I’ve put it out there, and now I wait for feedback. I’m genuinely happy if someone finds it useful. Even if the feedback is critical, it will help me improve.
Ultimately, this tool is a bridge. Bridges are meant to be crossed, tested, and strengthened over time. I’m excited to see where it leads.
Get the tool: https://github.com/armanwu/revit-to-sketchup-bridge

Today, architects can measure buildings in more detail than ever before. We can calculate energy use, daylight, temperature, structure, cost, circulation, and many other factors. Digital tools help us compare different options and find solutions that perform better. This is important progress because buildings should be safe, efficient, comfortable, and responsible toward the environment.
But good performance does not always create good architecture. A building can meet every technical target and still feel cold, confusing, or out of place. It may work well on paper but fail to create a meaningful experience for the people who use it.
What we can measure Many parts of a building can be measured. We can study how much daylight enters a room, how much energy the building uses, or how quickly people can reach an exit. We can compare materials, calculate costs, and predict indoor comfort. These measurements help architects make better decisions and reveal problems that may be difficult to see through intuition alone.
For example, a room may look bright in a rendering but receive too much heat during the day. A glass façade may look elegant but create high energy use, while a simple floor plan may produce long and inefficient walking routes. Data helps us see these problems more clearly and test possible solutions.
The danger begins when we assume that everything important can be measured in the same way.
What numbers cannot fully explain Architecture is not only about technical performance. It is also about how people feel, move, remember, and connect with a place. A room may have the correct temperature and enough daylight but still feel uncomfortable. A public space may have efficient circulation but feel unfriendly, and a house may use very little energy but fail to give its residents privacy, warmth, or a sense of belonging.
These qualities are difficult to turn into numbers. We can measure sound levels, but not always whether a space feels peaceful. We can measure the size of a window, but not fully explain the emotional effect of seeing a tree, a street, or the morning sky through it. We can also calculate how people move through a building, but not always what they feel during that movement.
This does not mean such qualities are mysterious or impossible to discuss. It means they need more than numbers. They also require observation, experience, conversation, and judgment.
When performance becomes the main goal Digital design tools often encourage us to optimize. We define a goal, test several options, and choose the one with the best result. This process is useful when the goal is clear, such as reducing energy use or improving daylight. In those cases, optimization can help architects find better solutions.
But architecture rarely has only one goal. A larger window may bring in more daylight, but it may also reduce privacy. A more efficient circulation route may remove moments of pause and discovery, while a highly optimized building form may perform well but feel disconnected from its surroundings. Every design decision includes several values at the same time, and not all of them can be measured.
The option with the highest score is not always the best design.
A building is experienced as a whole People do not experience buildings as separate performance results. They do not enter a room and think about its energy score, daylight percentage, or structural efficiency one by one. Instead, they experience the room as a whole, where light, sound, material, scale, temperature, memory, and meaning come together.
This is why architectural quality cannot be reduced to a checklist. A small weakness in one area may be acceptable if the space offers something valuable in another. A building is more than the sum of its technical parts, and those parts must work together to create a meaningful experience.
A building may perform well according to every measurable standard and still feel wrong because its parts do not create a convincing whole.
The role of architectural judgment As digital tools become more powerful, architectural judgment becomes more important, not less. Software can provide information, simulate performance, compare options, and show patterns that architects may not notice. But it cannot fully decide what kind of place people need or what qualities should matter most.
Those decisions require architects to understand people, culture, context, and the purpose of the building. The role of the architect is not to reject data, but to place data within a larger understanding of architecture. Good judgment asks not only whether a building performs well, but also whether it supports the lives of its users, belongs to its place, and creates comfort, dignity, and meaning.
These questions may not produce simple scores, but they still matter.
Beyond what we can measure We should continue measuring building performance. Better data can help us create safer, healthier, and more sustainable architecture. But measurement should support design, not define its full value.
Some of the most important qualities in architecture cannot be fully captured by a model, a simulation, or a spreadsheet. They appear through experience: in the way light changes during the day, in the feeling of entering a quiet room, or in the connection between a building and its surroundings.
A building can perform well and still feel wrong. The challenge for architects is not to choose between data and intuition, but to use both. We need to understand what numbers can tell us while remaining aware of what they leave out.
Good architecture needs performance, but it also needs judgment, care, and meaning.
summary:
Today, architects can measure buildings in more detail than ever before. We can calculate energy use, daylight, temperature, structure, cost, circulation, and many other factors. Digital tools help us compare different options and find solutions that perform better. This is important progress because buildings should be safe, efficient, comfortable, and responsible toward the environment.

But good performance does not always create good architecture. A building can meet every technical target and still feel cold, confusing, or out of place. It may work well on paper but fail to create a meaningful experience for the people who use it.
title: A Building Can Perform Well and Still Feel Wrong
