BIM is very good at describing buildings. A BIM model can store dimensions, materials, quantities, systems, and technical data. It can also help architects coordinate drawings, find clashes, and manage project information.
However, BIM is less effective at representing one important thing: design intent.
A model can show where a wall is located. It can store its thickness, material, fire rating, and other properties. But it usually does not explain why the architect placed the wall there, which options were considered, or what design value the decision was meant to protect.
BIM remembers what we decided. It does not always remember why.
Design begins with uncertainty Architectural design rarely begins with a complete answer. It often starts with questions, rough sketches, unclear ideas, and several possible directions. Architects need time to explore these possibilities before making final decisions.
BIM works differently. A BIM model needs clear objects and information. A wall needs a type, a room needs a boundary, and a parameter needs a value. This structure is useful because it helps architects create coordinated and reliable information.
Problems can appear, however, when this level of definition comes too early. An architect may begin choosing wall types, materials, and dimensions before the main design idea is clear. The model becomes more detailed, but the design may still be weak.
A precise model does not always mean a mature design.
Information is not the same as intention BIM is often described as an information-rich process. This is true, but more information does not always lead to more understanding.
For example, a BIM model may store a window’s size, material, cost, and thermal performance. But it may not explain that the window was placed to frame a view, bring morning light into a room, protect privacy, or create a visual connection with a garden.
These intentions may exist in sketches, diagrams, meetings, or the architect’s memory. They are important parts of the design, but they are often not stored in the BIM model.
The model represents the window. It does not fully represent the reason behind the window.
The appearance of certainty BIM can make a project look clear and complete. Drawings are coordinated, objects are aligned, and data is organized. Changes in the model can also appear automatically in plans, sections, schedules, and other views.
Because the model looks precise, we may begin to believe that the design is also fully resolved. This can be misleading. A detailed object may still come from a poor decision, and a coordinated model may still represent the wrong idea.
BIM does not force architects to make decisions too early. However, its structure can encourage us to define things before we have explored them enough.
Every design tool affects how we see a problem. BIM sees a building as a system of objects, properties, and relationships. This is useful, but it cannot represent every part of architecture equally well.
Some architectural qualities are easy to measure. Others, such as atmosphere, memory, meaning, and spatial experience, are much harder to place inside a parameter.
BIM is not the problem This is not an argument against BIM. BIM is an important tool for architectural coordination, documentation, construction, and building management.
The problem begins when we assume that the BIM model contains the whole design. It does not.
A building model can explain what will be built. A design process should also help us understand why it should be built in that way.
Architects therefore need other forms of representation. Sketches, diagrams, physical models, written notes, and design alternatives can preserve ideas that BIM cannot easily store.
The goal is not to replace BIM. The goal is to understand what BIM can represent well and what still needs other tools.
Keeping the reasons behind decisions We do not need to place every design thought inside the BIM model. That would make the process more complicated and create more unnecessary information.
However, important decisions should not lose their reasons. A project team can record the problem behind a decision, the options that were considered, the reason for choosing one option, and the architectural value that should be protected.
This information becomes especially useful when a project moves from one person or team to another. A decision may be clear to the original architect, but without an explanation, another person may see it as unnecessary or arbitrary.
When the reason disappears, the decision becomes easier to change or remove.
Beyond object modeling The future of BIM should not only be about adding more objects, data, and automation. It should also help project teams understand important design decisions.
A wall should still be represented as a wall. But the project record could also explain what problem the wall solves, which options were explored, why the final option was selected, and what architectural quality it protects.
This is not only a software problem. It is also a question of how architects think, communicate, and remember.
Perhaps BIM should not only support object modeling. It should also support decision modeling.
What should BIM remember? BIM represents buildings well because buildings can be divided into objects, systems, properties, and information. Design intent is more difficult to represent because it can change during the project and may come from discussion, experience, intuition, and judgment.
BIM may never represent every part of architectural thinking. But it should help us preserve the reasons behind important decisions.
A building is more than a collection of modeled objects. It is also the result of decisions about people, place, space, performance, and meaning.
BIM can tell us what a building contains. A better design process should also help us remember why those things are there.
summary:
BIM is very good at describing buildings. A BIM model can store dimensions, materials, quantities, systems, and technical data. It can also help architects coordinate drawings, find clashes, and manage project information.

However, BIM is less effective at representing one important thing: design intent.

A model can show where a wall is located. It can store its thickness, material, fire rating, and other properties. But it usually does not explain why the architect placed the wall there, which options were considered, or what design value the decision was meant to protect.
title: BIM Represents Buildings Better Than It Represents Design Intent

Concept & The Soft Explosion Shard Museum explores the tension between aggressive geometry and tactile warmth. While traditional museums are often static, monolithic boxes, this project envisions a cultural space that radiates outward like a cluster of crystals growing from a reflecting pool. To keep its sharp, overhanging shards from feeling hostile, the faceted envelope is wrapped in warm vertical timber slats—creating a “soft explosion” that balances mathematical precision with natural materiality.
The Computational Logic: Tilted & Twisted Prisms The geometry is generated by a custom script in Julia. Rather than modeling a single static block, the algorithm builds the museum through a five-step transformation of a triangular prism, then collides four distinct shard volumes into one cohesive composition:
From Triangular Base to Twisted Shard (Steps 1–5): Each volume starts with a randomized three-point triangular footprint on the ground plane (15 to 25 meters wide) and is extruded vertically to its target height (h). The top triangle is then pushed sideways (Δx, Δy) to create a dramatic lean and rotated around its center (θz) to introduce a twist—while splitting each side wall diagonally into two flat triangles so every surface stays completely planar. Four-Mass Collision (A + B + C + D): To create the final museum volume, the script intersects four configured shards around a central origin: a 35-meter Primary Mass (A), a 25-meter Left Collision (B) leaning outward, a 20-meter Front Collision (C) jutting toward the plaza, and a 45-meter Vertical Spire (D) anchoring the skyline. View Julia Source Code (shard_museum.jl)using GLMakie using GeometryBasics using Random using Colors # Initialize the 3D visualization environment fig = Figure( size=(960, 1000), backgroundcolor=:white ) # Configure the 3D architectural visualization ax = Axis3( fig[1, 1], aspect=:data, azimuth=0.6π, elevation=0.15π ) # Hide axis decorations and spines hidedecorations!(ax) hidespines!(ax) # Generate an inclined and twisted triangular prism function create_sharp_prism( center_x, center_y, height, tilt_x, tilt_y, rotation_z ) # Define the randomized width of the triangular base base_width = rand(15.0:25.0) # Generate three vertices forming the triangular base base_points = [ Point3f( center_x + rand(-5:5), center_y + rand(-5:5), 0 ), Point3f( center_x + base_width, center_y + rand(-5:5), 0 ), Point3f( center_x + rand(0:5), center_y + base_width, 0 ) ] # Calculate horizontal displacement based on height and inclination offset_x = tilt_x * height offset_y = tilt_y * height # Generate the upper triangular surface roof_points = [ point + Point3f(offset_x, offset_y, height) for point in base_points ] # Calculate rotation components around the vertical Z-axis cos_angle = cos(rotation_z) sin_angle = sin(rotation_z) # Calculate the geometric center of the upper surface roof_center = sum(roof_points) / 3 # Initialize the collection of rotated upper vertices rotated_roof_points = Point3f[] # Rotate the upper vertices around their geometric center # The triangular base remains stationary for point in roof_points # Calculate local coordinates relative to the roof center dx = point[1] - roof_center[1] dy = point[2] - roof_center[2] # Apply the rotation transformation rotated_x = dx * cos_angle - dy * sin_angle + roof_center[1] rotated_y = dx * sin_angle + dy * cos_angle + roof_center[2] # Store the transformed upper vertex push!( rotated_roof_points, Point3f( rotated_x, rotated_y, point[3] ) ) end # Combine the base and upper vertices # Vertices 1-3 define the triangular base # Vertices 4-6 define the transformed upper surface all_points = [ base_points; rotated_roof_points ] # Construct the triangular faces of the prism faces = [ # Bottom triangular surface GLTriangleFace(1, 2, 3), # Top triangular surface GLTriangleFace(4, 6, 5), # First lateral surface GLTriangleFace(1, 2, 5), GLTriangleFace(1, 5, 4), # Second lateral surface GLTriangleFace(2, 3, 6), GLTriangleFace(2, 6, 5), # Third lateral surface GLTriangleFace(3, 1, 4), GLTriangleFace(3, 4, 6) ] # Construct and return the final architectural mesh return GeometryBasics.Mesh( all_points, faces ) end # Initialize the architectural massing composition println("Generating Deconstructivist Museum...") # Define a titanium-inspired metallic color palette titanium_palette = [ # Zinc Grey RGBAf(0.6, 0.65, 0.7, 0.9), # Dark Metal RGBAf(0.5, 0.55, 0.6, 0.9), # Light Aluminium RGBAf(0.7, 0.75, 0.8, 0.8), # Contrast Dark RGBAf(0.2, 0.25, 0.3, 0.95) ] # Define four intersecting architectural masses # Each configuration contains: # center_x, center_y, height, tilt_x, tilt_y, rotation_z mass_configurations = [ # Primary architectural mass (0, 0, 35.0, 0.4, 0.2, 0.2), # Secondary mass intersecting from the left (-10, 5, 25.0, -0.5, 0.1, -0.3), # Secondary mass intersecting from the front (5, -10, 20.0, 0.1, -0.6, 0.5), # Tall inclined architectural spire (0, 0, 45.0, -0.2, -0.2, 0.8) ] # Generate the architectural composition for (index, configuration) in enumerate(mass_configurations) # Extract geometric transformation parameters center_x, center_y, height, tilt_x, tilt_y, rotation_z = configuration # Generate the inclined and twisted triangular prism architectural_mass = create_sharp_prism( center_x, center_y, height, tilt_x, tilt_y, rotation_z ) # Select the corresponding metallic material color material_color = titanium_palette[ mod1(index, length(titanium_palette)) ] # Render the solid architectural geometry # FastShading provides basic surface illumination # Specular controls the intensity of reflected highlights # Shininess controls the appearance of metallic reflections mesh!( ax, architectural_mass, color=material_color, shading=FastShading, specular=Vec3f(0.8), shininess=10.0f0 ) # Highlight the geometric edges using a white wireframe # The wireframe emphasizes angularity and geometric fragmentation wireframe!( ax, architectural_mass, color=(:white, 0.6), linewidth=1.5 ) end # Optional human-scale reference # Concept & Urban Tectonics Chaos Crystal investigates how a purely mathematical coordinate transformation can be disciplined into a buildable civic landmark. Rather than sculpting deconstructivist forms by hand, the project begins with an analytical sphere and subjects it to controlled radial perturbation—producing an expressive crystalline silhouette that anchors a stepped urban plaza.
To ground its aggressive geometry within the city fabric, the building is organized as a tectonic dialogue between three primary systems: a heavy, board-formed concrete base that absorbs pedestrian circulation from the plaza; an interlocking opaque shell of matte charcoal titanium-zinc panels; and triangular structural glass apertures that slice across the folds to reveal the warm, multi-level public atrium within.
The Computational Logic: From Sphere to Crystal The form-finding workflow is written in Julia, transforming a simple mathematical sphere into a faceted building envelope through four clear geometric steps:
Coarse Spherical Grid (12 × 12 Resolution): Instead of a high-density mesh that would create noisy surface ripples, the script divides a sphere of radius 12.0 into a deliberate 12 × 12 grid. At this coarse scale, every grid cell naturally becomes the size of a full architectural facade facet. Controlled Radial Push and Pull (-5.0 to +15.0): Every point on the sphere is pushed outward or pulled inward by a random distance between -5.0 and +15.0 units. Inward pulls carve deep alcoves and valleys, while outward pushes project dramatic cantilevered spires. Flattening the Base on the Ground (Z = 0): The entire crystal is lifted +10.0 units upward, and any point falling below ground level is automatically flattened to Z = 0. This single rule turns the bottom of the floating sphere into a stable, flat floor plate on the plaza. Closing the Surface with Flat Triangles: Finally, the script stitches the seams and poles together and divides every four-sided grid cell into two flat triangular faces—ensuring a completely closed, buildable volume. View Julia Source Code (chaos_crystal.jl)using GLMakie using GeometryBasics using Random using Colors # Create the 3D drawing environment fig = Figure(size=(800, 800)) ax = Axis3( fig[1, 1], aspect=:data, azimuth=(-π / 2), elevation=0, perspectiveness=0 ) hidedecorations!(ax) hidespines!(ax) # Create the ground plane wireframe!( ax, Rect3f(Point3f(-30, -30, 0), Vec3f(60, 60, 0)), color=(:white, 0.1), linewidth=0.0 ) # Generate the Chaos Crystal geometry function chaos_crystal() # Define the main parameters resolution = 12 base_radius = 12 # Initialize mesh data points = Point3f[] faces = GLTriangleFace[] # Create a grid to store 3D points grid_points = Matrix{Point3f}(undef, resolution, resolution) # Generate points using spherical coordinates for i in 1:resolution for j in 1:resolution theta = π * (i - 1) / (resolution - 1) phi = 2π * (j - 1) / (resolution - 1) # Apply random radius variation random_radius = base_radius + rand(-5.0:15.0) # Convert spherical coordinates into Cartesian coordinates x = random_radius * sin(theta) * cos(phi) y = random_radius * sin(theta) * sin(phi) z = random_radius * cos(theta) # Raise the geometry above ground final_z = max(z + 10, 0) grid_points[i, j] = Point3f(x, y, final_z) end end # Close the spherical surface for i in 1:resolution grid_points[i, resolution] = grid_points[i, 1] end # Connect the top and bottom poles for j in 1:resolution grid_points[1, j] = grid_points[1, 1] grid_points[resolution, j] = grid_points[resolution, 1] end # Connect neighboring points to create triangular faces for i in 1:(resolution-1) for j in 1:(resolution-1) p1 = grid_points[i, j] p2 = grid_points[i, j+1] p3 = grid_points[i+1, j+1] p4 = grid_points[i+1, j] push!(points, p1, p2, p3, p4) # Divide each quadrilateral into two outward-facing triangles current = length(points) - 3 push!( faces, GLTriangleFace(current, current + 3, current + 2), GLTriangleFace(current + 2, current + 1, current) ) end end # Return the final 3D mesh return GeometryBasics.Mesh(points, faces) end # Generate the crystal crystal_mesh = chaos_crystal() # Display the solid surface mesh!( ax, crystal_mesh, color=(RGB(0.50, 0.70, 0.68), 0.9), shading=true ) # Display the mesh edges wireframe!( ax, crystal_mesh, color=(:black, 0.28), linewidth=1.2 ) # Render the final result display(fig) Why Triangles Matter: From Elevation to Physical Model A classic challenge in freeform architecture is building complex surfaces without expensive curved glass or twisted metal panels. Because a four-sided polygon almost always warps when its corners move randomly, the Julia script explicitly splits every grid cell into triangles.
In the script, the 3D camera is set to a pure orthographic front view—allowing the raw Julia output to translate directly into a scaled architectural elevation drawing. Resting firmly on the flat Z = 0 ground line, the large triangular facets are broken down into human-scaled building systems: a board-formed concrete base at street level, standing-seam titanium-zinc panels across the solid peaks, and subdivided curtain-wall glazing.
Because any three points in space always form a perfectly flat plane, the entire building skin can be cut from flat sheets. As shown in the physical study model above—built from grey museum board, flat acrylic glazing, and a stepped basswood plaza—the geometry from Julia translates directly into physical construction without a single curved panel.
Interior Space & Light Inside, the sharp exterior shell opens up into a bright, multi-level public atrium where the triangular geometry becomes the main structural expression:
Sloped Concrete Piers & Skybridges: Massive cast-in-place concrete piers support the upper exhibition galleries, linked across the central void by slender steel bridges that let visitors experience the space from different heights. Triangulated Skylights & Acoustic Ceilings: Where the shell opens toward the sky, angled steel mullions follow the triangular mesh lines, while the solid peaks are lined with warm-lit acoustic panels that bounce daylight deep into the concourse. Along the outer edge of the building, the outward-pushed points of the crystal become triple-height viewing galleries where walkways and stairs meet right behind the glass facade. From here, the steel diagrid joints frame diagonal views back down to the stepped plaza and out toward the city skyline while casting long afternoon shadow patterns across the floor.
From the upper mezzanine walkway, the relationship between the outer shell and the inner concrete frame becomes clear. Inclined concrete columns support the cantilevered gallery floors, while a central stair and escalator spine draws visitors upward through the folded volume.
Day-to-Night Transformation While the Julia script only calculates spherical coordinates and random radial distances, architectural interpretation turns that raw mesh into an experience of light and time. By day, the crystal reads as a heavy, sculptural monolith carved by shadow. At dusk, that reading flips completely—warm light from the galleries glows outward through the triangular glass facets while subtle linear lights trace the folded seams, turning the building into a welcoming lantern on the public plaza.

Concept & The Porous High-Rise Eroded Monolith challenges the sealed, air-conditioned box of conventional high-rise architecture. Positioned at a prominent urban street corner, the project asks what happens when we subtract a massive three-dimensional void out of a rigid modernist grid—opening the heart of the tower to daylight, cross-breezes, and stepped communal gardens.
The Computational Logic: Carving with Distance Written in Julia, the form-finding workflow uses a subtractive method rather than stacking blocks upward. As shown in the concept diagram below, the algorithm sculpts the tower by subtracting an invisible sphere from a solid grid of cubes:
A Solid Voxel Tower (11 × 11 × 21 Blocks): The building begins as a complete 3D matrix of 2,541 cubic modules (x and y from -5 to 5, and z from 0 to 20), establishing a disciplined orthogonal tower envelope. The Spherical Cutter (Radius = 7.0): An invisible cutting sphere is centered along the front corner edge at mid-height (x = 5, y = 5, z = 10). For every cube in the tower, the script measures its straight-line distance (d) to the center of the sphere and removes any block where d ≤ 7.0. Progressive Real-Time Growth: Using Julia’s live visualization stream, the remaining blocks assemble floor by floor from the ground up and are shaded along an ice-blue gradient according to their distance from the carved void. View Julia Source Code (eroded_monolith.jl)using GLMakie using GeometryBasics using LinearAlgebra # Define the voxel grid boundaries x_range = -5:5 y_range = -5:5 z_range = 0:20 # Define the spherical cutting tool cutter_center = Point3f(5, 5, 10) cutter_radius = 7.0 # Initialize observable data for real-time visualization voxels_live = Observable(Point3f[]) colors_live = Observable(Float64[]) # Create the visualization figure and 3D scene fig = Figure(size=(1000, 1000)) ax = LScene(fig[1, 1]) # Define the site boundary as a transparent wireframe box site_bounds = Rect3f(Vec3f(-7, -7, 0), Vec3f(14, 14, 21)) wireframe!(ax, site_bounds, color=:grey30, linewidth=0.2, transparency=true) # Visualize voxels using individual cube markers # Color intensity represents the distance from the cutting tool center meshscatter!(ax, voxels_live, marker=Rect3f(Vec3f(-0.5), Vec3f(1)), markersize=1.0, color=colors_live, colormap=:ice, colorrange=(0, 15), ) # Display the initial visualization display(fig) # Execute the voxel generation process asynchronously @async begin println("Starting voxel generation...") # Create temporary arrays to store voxel positions and colors temp_voxels = Point3f[] temp_colors = Float64[] # Iterate through the entire 3D voxel grid for z in z_range for x in x_range for y in y_range # Define the current voxel position point = Point3f(x, y, z) # Calculate the Euclidean distance from the cutting tool center distance = norm(point - cutter_center) # Retain voxels located outside the spherical cutting region if distance > cutter_radius push!(temp_voxels, point) push!(temp_colors, distance) # Update the visualization in real time voxels_live[] = temp_voxels colors_live[] = temp_colors # Introduce a short delay for progressive visualization sleep(0.00001) end end end # Allow the rendering process to refresh between layers sleep(0.00001) end println("Voxel generation completed!") end Architectural Translation: The Carved Vertical Park While the Julia script simply filters out cubes within a 7.0-unit radius, architectural interpretation turns that stepped mathematical cavity into a dramatic public and bioclimatic heart for the building:
Outer Grid vs. Inner Canyon: The untouched outer faces of the tower keep a clean concrete-and-glass curtain wall anchored by dark stone piers at street level. Where the sphere cuts into the corner, the exposed voxel steps are clad in warm weathered Corten steel and board-formed concrete—visually expressing the “cut” as if a geological layer has been exposed. Stepped Amphitheater Gardens: The lower half of the carved sphere naturally forms a cascading series of planted terraces and outdoor stairs, while the upper half creates a dramatic stepped concrete soffit that shelters the gardens below from direct rain and midday sun. Experience Inside the Void Standing on the elevated timber deck inside the carved corner, the abstract voxel grid becomes a tangible spatial experience. Overhead, the stepped concrete ceiling recalls the cubic resolution of the Julia algorithm, while double-height glass walls connect the indoor workspaces directly to the planted terraces. Rather than isolating occupants behind a sealed glass facade, the eroded corner frames panoramic views down the tree-lined boulevard at sunset—turning a simple distance formula into a living vertical park.

Concept & Vaulted Tectonics Flux Vaults investigates how serial mathematical variation can generate a monumental vaulted civic concourse. Rather than treating a long-span roof as a uniform extrusion, the project conceives the building envelope as a rhythmic sequence of offset semicircular shells that rise, widen, and shift laterally along a 100-meter axis—creating an interlocking topography of board-formed concrete arches and glazed clerestory crescents poised above a reflecting water basin.
The Computational Logic: Parametric Arches Written in Julia, the script builds the shell by generating a row of semicircular arches along a straight spine and connecting them into a continuous surface:
A Row of 30 Arches (100 m Length): A 100-meter axis is divided into 30 equally spaced arch ribs, with each arch curve plotted using 30 points from one side to the other. Varying Width, Height, and Shift: Instead of repeating identical arches, the script randomly varies three dimensions for each rib—its span width (5 to 15 units), its peak height (4 to 20 units), and its sideways shift (-5 to +5 units). Grounded Arch Geometry: Each arch curve is drawn using simple sine and cosine waves. Because a half-sine wave always starts and ends at zero, every arch—no matter how tall, wide, or shifted—lands both of its feet cleanly on the flat ground plane (Z = 0). Connecting Ribs into a Shell: Finally, the script connects each arch to its neighbor with a grid of flat triangles, creating a continuous vaulted roof structure. View Julia Source Code (flux_vaults.jl)using GLMakie using GeometryBasics using Colors using Random # Initialize the 3D visualization environment fig = Figure(size=(1000, 600), backgroundcolor=:grey10) ax = Axis3(fig[1, 1], aspect=:data, azimuth=0.4π, elevation=0.2π) hidedecorations!(ax) hidespines!(ax) # Create the ground plane wireframe!(ax, Rect3f(Point3f(-10, -30, 0), Vec3f(120, 60, 0)), linewidth=0.0 ) # Generate a parametric building structure using a series of irregular ribs function generate_building() # Define the main geometric parameters building_length = 100 rib_count = 30 curve_resolution = 30 # Initialize geometry containers points = Point3f[] faces = GLTriangleFace[] ribs_data = Vector{Point3f}[] # Generate individual curved ribs along the building length for i in 1:rib_count # Define the position and random dimensions of each rib position_x = (i - 1) * (building_length / rib_count) width = rand(5.0:15.0) height = rand(4.0:20.0) offset_y = rand(-5.0:5.0) # Generate points along a semicircular profile rib_points = Point3f[] for j in 1:curve_resolution theta = π * (j - 1) / (curve_resolution - 1) y = offset_y - (width * cos(theta)) z = height * sin(theta) push!(rib_points, Point3f(position_x, y, z)) end # Store the generated rib geometry push!(ribs_data, rib_points) end # Connect adjacent ribs to generate the building surface index_counter = 1 for i in 1:(rib_count-1) current_rib = ribs_data[i] next_rib = ribs_data[i+1] # Construct triangular faces between neighboring ribs for j in 1:(curve_resolution-1) p1 = current_rib[j] p2 = next_rib[j] p3 = next_rib[j+1] p4 = current_rib[j+1] # Add vertices to the geometry push!(points, p1, p2, p3, p4) # Define two triangular faces for each surface segment push!(faces, GLTriangleFace(index_counter, index_counter + 1, index_counter + 2)) push!(faces, GLTriangleFace(index_counter + 2, index_counter + 3, index_counter)) index_counter += 4 end end # Return the completed building mesh return GeometryBasics.Mesh(points, faces) end # Generate the building geometry building_mesh = generate_building() # Render the translucent building surface mesh!(ax, building_mesh, color=(:teal, 0.5), transparency=true, shading=true ) # Display the structural wireframe wireframe!(ax, building_mesh, color=(:white, 0.4), linewidth=1.0 ) # Display the final 3D visualization display(fig) From Wireframe Mesh to Physical Model To turn the continuous digital mesh into a buildable roof structure, neighboring ribs are grouped into overlapping vault shells separated by crescent-shaped glass skylights.
As shown in the physical study model above—built from layered grey museum-board arches, segmented white shell panels, basswood bases, and radial acrylic glazing—dividing each arch into 30 straight segments allows the curved vaults to be constructed from simple flat panel strips and standard arch ribs.
Interior Concourse & Evening Atmosphere Inside the building, the height differences (4 to 20 meters) and sideways shifts between consecutive arches become the main architectural feature:
Monumental Concrete Arches: Thick board-formed concrete arch ribs carry the roof loads down to the floor while framing a wide, column-free public hall with escalators and an upper mezzanine bridge. Crescent Skylights: Wherever one arch rises higher or shifts sideways next to its neighbor, the gap between them is filled with curved clerestory glass—washing the concrete vaults with natural daylight and opening views out to the surrounding water. While the Julia script simply randomizes arch widths, heights, and offsets along a line, architectural interpretation turns those numbers into a physical rhythm of expansion and compression as people walk through the 100-meter hall. At dusk, warm uplighting washes the underside of the concrete arches while interior light glows through the glazed entrance and crescent skylights, mirroring the vaults across the still water basin.

Concept & Modular Porosity Jenga Village explores how simple geometric rules can break the monotony of repetitive modular housing while recapturing the spatial warmth of an organic tropical kampong. Where conventional apartment blocks rely on uniform vertical stacks, this study tests how slight horizontal shifts, varied room proportions, and fixed angular rotations can turn simple boxes into a porous “vertical village” filled with shaded alleys, courtyards, and roof terraces.
The Computational Logic: Rule-Based Stacking Written in Julia, the script organizes the neighborhood on a 4 × 4 plot grid using a 10-meter base module and a 4-meter story height. As illustrated in the workflow diagram below, the algorithm transforms a flat site grid into an interlocking village cluster by applying four simple geometric rules to every block:
Grid & Vertical Stacking (1 to 3 Floors): Across the 4 × 4 plot grid, each site is randomly assigned between one and three stories—creating an undulating roofscape that lets daylight and breeze reach the center of the cluster. Block Proportion & Elongation (0.7× to 1.8×): Instead of identical cubes, each block is stretched or narrowed along its length (1.0× to 1.8×) and width (0.7× to 1.0×) to accommodate different room sizes and dwelling layouts. Fixed Angular Rotation (0°, 15°, 30°, 45°, 90°): Rather than chaotic angles, each volume turns around its vertical axis using five clean construction angles, opening up diagonal views and pocket courtyards between neighboring homes. Horizontal Displacement (±2.5 m): As units stack upward, each floor shifts horizontally on X and Y by up to 2.5 meters—creating cantilevers that shade the walkways below while exposing the roof beneath as an outdoor terrace. View Julia Source Code (jenga_village.jl)using GLMakie using GeometryBasics using Random using Colors # Initialize the random generation system seed = 2026 rng = MersenneTwister(seed) # Initialize the 3D visualization environment fig = Figure( size=(900, 900), backgroundcolor=:white ) view_limits = (-15, 60, -15, 60, 0, 25) ax = Axis3( fig[1, 1], aspect=:data, limits=view_limits, perspectiveness=0.05, azimuth=0.25π, elevation=0.2π ) # Hide axis decorations and spines hidedecorations!(ax) hidespines!(ax) # Display the visualization window display(fig) # Define the basic architectural parameters block_size = 10.0 floor_height = 4.0 grid_count_x = 4 grid_count_y = 4 grid_spacing = 1.3 min_floors = 1 max_floors = 3 # Define the generative transformation parameters rotation_angles = [0, 15, 30, 45, 90] length_factors = [1.0, 1.0, 1.3, 1.5, 1.8] width_factors = [0.7, 0.8, 1.0, 1.0] max_displacement = 2.5 # Define the architectural color palette color_palette = [ RGBAf(0.0, 0.8, 0.9, 0.9), RGBAf(0.0, 0.5, 0.6, 0.9), RGBAf(0.2, 0.7, 0.6, 0.9), RGBAf(0.6, 0.65, 0.7, 0.9) ] # Create a rotated architectural block function create_rotated_block!( ax, center_x, center_y, base_z, length_x, width_y, height_z, angle, block_color ) # Convert the rotation angle to radians theta = deg2rad(angle) # Calculate the rotation components cos_theta = cos(theta) sin_theta = sin(theta) # Define the local block corners local_corners = [ (-length_x / 2, -width_y / 2), ( length_x / 2, -width_y / 2), ( length_x / 2, width_y / 2), (-length_x / 2, width_y / 2) ] # Rotate the block corners around the vertical axis rotated_corners = Point3f[] for (local_x, local_y) in local_corners rotated_x = center_x + local_x * cos_theta - local_y * sin_theta rotated_y = center_y + local_x * sin_theta + local_y * cos_theta push!( rotated_corners, Point3f(rotated_x, rotated_y, base_z) ) end # Generate the bottom and top vertices vertices = Point3f[] for point in rotated_corners push!(vertices, point) end for point in rotated_corners push!( vertices, Point3f(point[1], point[2], base_z + height_z) ) end # Define the triangular faces of the block faces = [ 1 3 2; 1 4 3; 5 6 7; 5 7 8; 1 2 6; 1 6 5; 2 3 7; 2 7 6; 3 4 8; 3 8 7; 4 1 5; 4 5 8 ] # Convert the face indices into triangle faces triangle_faces = [ TriangleFace{Int}( faces[i, 1], faces[i, 2], faces[i, 3] ) for i in 1:size(faces, 1) ] # Construct the rotated block geometry block_mesh = GeometryBasics.Mesh( vertices, triangle_faces ) # Render the architectural mass mesh!( ax, block_mesh, color=block_color, shading=true ) # Define the twelve visible block edges edge_pairs = [ (1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 4), (4, 1), (5, 6), (6, 7), (7, 8), (8, 5), (1, 5), (2, 6), (3, 7), (4, 8) ] # Draw the architectural outlines for (start_index, end_index) in edge_pairs lines!( ax, [ vertices[start_index], vertices[end_index] ], color=:black, linewidth=1.0 ) end end # Generate the architectural village asynchronously @async begin # Iterate through the horizontal village grid for x in 1:grid_count_x for y in 1:grid_count_y # Randomly determine the building height floor_count = rand( rng, min_floors:max_floors ) # Calculate the building grid position base_x = (x - 1) * block_size * grid_spacing base_y = (y - 1) * block_size * grid_spacing # Generate the stacked building masses for z in 1:floor_count # Calculate the vertical position pos_z = (z - 1) * floor_height # Generate random horizontal displacements offset_x = ( rand(rng) * 2 - 1 ) * max_displacement offset_y = ( rand(rng) * 2 - 1 ) * max_displacement # Generate random block dimensions length_factor = rand(rng, length_factors) width_factor = rand(rng, width_factors) length_x = block_size * length_factor width_y = block_size * width_factor # Randomly select a rotation angle rotation_angle = rand( rng, rotation_angles ) # Calculate the center of the architectural mass center_x = base_x + block_size / 2 + offset_x center_y = base_y + block_size / 2 + offset_y # Randomly select the architectural color block_color = rand( rng, color_palette ) # Generate the transformed architectural block create_rotated_block!( ax, center_x, center_y, pos_z, length_x, width_y, floor_height, rotation_angle, block_color ) # Animate the construction sequence sleep(0.1) end end # Pause between village grid columns sleep(0.2) end end From Digital Blocks to Physical Study Model Because the script builds every unit as a clean rectangular box rotated to a fixed angle (15°, 30°, 45°, or 90°), every module remains straightforward to build despite the organic look of the overall village.
In the physical study model above, the color-coded blocks from the Julia script are translated into a clear two-part structural hierarchy using grey museum board and basswood:
Heavy Structural Cores (Grey Volumes): Flat-roofed concrete and masonry bases anchor the corners of each plot, supporting the cantilevered blocks above while providing flat roof decks for upper-level terraces. Lightweight Timber Pavilions (Wood Volumes): The rotated upper blocks become warm timber-framed living spaces with sloped roofs, window sunshades, and open pergolas, connected across the gaps between plots by exterior stairways. Vernacular Materiality & Courtyard Life While the Julia code only arranges geometric boxes in space, architectural interpretation turns those shifted volumes into a livable tropical neighborhood:
Tropical Material Palette: The four block colors in the script are interpreted as a layered local palette—exposed concrete frames, red-brick ground walls, natural stone retaining walls, and timber upper floors shaded by woven bamboo trellises. Pocket Courtyards & Exterior Stairs: The spacing between the 4 × 4 plots and the angled rotations naturally carve out communal pocket gardens, shaded pedestrian lanes, and stone staircases that weave through the village. Living on the Terraces From inside the upper homes, the 2.5-meter horizontal shifts and angled rotations create a generous domestic experience. Whenever an upper block slides or turns over the unit below, the exposed lower roof becomes a private balcony or garden terrace. Instead of looking straight into a neighbor’s window, sliding timber doors open diagonally across the shared green courtyard.
At dusk, warm light from the timber windows and string-lit roof pergolas brings the stepped terraces and pedestrian alleys to life—turning a simple 4 × 4 computational grid into an intimate, human-scaled community.

Concept & Spatial Collision Titanium Clash explores the boundary between algorithmic randomness and architectural order. Drawing inspiration from deconstructivist form-making, the project tests how a simple script can generate high-energy spatial collisions—where sharp, soaring spires pierce and counter-balance one another above a calm reflecting pool.
The Computational Logic: Stochastic Shard Aggregation Instead of starting with a manual sketch or a clay model, this study begins with a script in Julia that builds a complex deconstructivist massing by aggregating eight irregular tetrahedral shards around a shared origin:
Tetrahedral Geometry Logic (p1, p2, p3 + apex): Each shard is constructed from four randomized points—three base vertices scattered near ground level (x, y ∈ [-35, 35], z ∈ [-5, 5]) and one elevated apex projected high into the air (x, y ∈ [-55, 55], z ∈ [60, 85]). Connecting these four points forms an irregular four-face tetrahedron whose surfaces are always flat triangles. Sequential Aggregation Loop (1 to 8 Shards): In an iterative loop (i = 1 to 8), eight independent shards are generated around Point3f(0, 0, 0). As the loop progresses from a single pyramid to the full eight-shard cluster, the leaning volumes pierce and interlock with one another—rendered in a four-tone metallic slate palette with crisp white wireframe edges. The rise of AI in architecture raises a critical question: How do we merge the intuitive intelligence built over years of practice with the logic of algorithms? Both are powerful forces. But for them to work in harmony, architects must learn to wield these tools effectively, rather than being replaced by them.
To thrive in this new era, architects need to cultivate specific technical skills that bridge the gap between creative intuition and computational power.
1. Programming and Algorithmic Thinking Programming is the language of AI. To truly control how an AI generates design solutions, understanding the code behind it is essential. Python has become the industry standard, offering a gateway to powerful AI libraries like TensorFlow and PyTorch without an overly steep learning curve.
Why it matters: Programming gives you agency. In generative design, for example, writing your own scripts allows you to define constraints that align with your specific aesthetic vision, ensuring the output isn’t just random data. The Visual Route: For those who prefer not to write raw code, visual programming tools like Grasshopper (Rhino) or Dynamo (Revit) offer a perfect alternative. They allow architects to build complex algorithmic logic by connecting visual nodes, making AI accessible within the design workflow. 2. Machine Learning and Data Science Machine Learning (ML) is essentially about teaching computers to learn from patterns. For architects, this capability is invaluable for predicting building performance long before construction begins.
Performance Prediction: Imagine training a model on data from your previous projects. The AI could learn to forecast energy efficiency or structural loads for a new design instantly—a crucial capability for sustainable architecture. Data-Driven Decisions: This requires a grasp of Data Science. Architects today handle massive datasets, from climate metrics to user behavior. Familiarity with tools like Pandas helps organize this information, while data visualization allows you to spot patterns and make informed, objective design decisions. 3. Generative Design and Parametrics Generative design shifts the workflow from “drawing” to “curating.” By inputting constraints—such as site boundaries, sunlight requirements, or budget—AI can generate hundreds of optimized iterations.
Expanding Exploration: Platforms like Autodesk Generative Design allow us to test forms that might be impossible to conceive manually. It accelerates the exploration phase, presenting massing options that optimize for factors like daylight and ventilation in seconds. The Parametric Foundation: This relies heavily on parametric design logic. Understanding how changing a single parameter (like window geometry) impacts the entire building system allows for rapid experimentation and refinement without the need to redraw from scratch. 4. Intelligent BIM Workflows BIM is already a standard, but AI elevates it from a static model to an intelligent assistant.
Proactive Analysis: AI can scan BIM models to predict potential maintenance issues or structural weaknesses early in the design phase. Enhanced Clash Detection: Beyond simply spotting where pipes intersect with beams, AI can suggest solutions based on historical data from successful projects. Cost and Schedule Accuracy: By learning from real-world construction data, AI can provide more realistic estimates on costs and timelines, helping architects mitigate the risk of delays and budget overruns. Conclusion AI is a powerful engine for efficiency, but it cannot replace the architect’s eye. That human sense of what feels “right”—our intuition—remains irreplaceable. The architects who will succeed in this era are those who can synthesize their artistic instincts with these intelligent algorithms, creating designs that are not only efficient but deeply meaningful.

As an architect and daily user of Building Information Modeling (BIM), I am the first to admit its tremendous value. It has undeniably revolutionized how we handle efficiency and quality in architectural projects. But here is the thing: if we want this technology to keep evolving, we cannot afford to turn a blind eye to its flaws.
Being a BIM advocate doesn’t mean accepting it blindly. In fact, pointing out where BIM falls short is exactly what we need to drive the industry forward.
The Undeniable Benefits I have seen firsthand how BIM transforms the workflow. The biggest win is clearly collaboration. With a single integrated model, the whole team works in sync, drastically reducing those communication errors that used to plague complex projects.
Then there is the visualization aspect. BIM gives us realistic 3D models that help clients actually understand the design, leading to faster, better decisions. Beyond just pretty pictures, the data integrity—from structural analysis to energy efficiency—allows us to make informed decisions based on hard facts, not just guesses. It creates a “single source of truth” where everyone has access to the same up-to-date information, minimizing version conflicts.
Why We Must Embrace Criticism However, just because BIM is powerful doesn’t mean it is perfect. It is crucial that we, as practitioners, don’t ignore its shortcomings.
Critiquing BIM isn’t about attacking the technology; it’s about debugging it. By accepting criticism, we open ourselves to new perspectives. We might find that interoperability between different platforms is still a nightmare, or that modeling complex geometry is clunkier than it should be.
If we stop complaining about these issues, developers stop fixing them. Constructive criticism provides the roadmap for innovation. It forces us to ask difficult questions, which in turn leads to better solutions and more efficient workflows. We need an environment where questioning the tools is encouraged, not silenced.
Context is Everything We also need to be realistic about context. You cannot simply force a standard BIM workflow into every project or every country and expect it to work perfectly.
Work culture, local habits, and specific project requirements play a huge role. BIM needs to be flexible. The way a firm in Europe uses BIM might not fit the workflow of a studio in Indonesia. We need to adapt the implementation strategies to fit the local reality, rather than rigidly following a manual.
This requires open dialogue—not just among architects, but with software developers too. By sharing our real-world struggles, we can help shape tools that actually fit our diverse working environments.
Conclusion To push architecture forward, we need to stay open-minded. Criticism is not a sign of rejection; it is a catalyst for improvement. By honestly identifying the weaknesses in our current BIM tools and workflows, we can push for a future where technology serves the design process, not the other way around. Let’s keep the feedback loop open.

We live in a world that changes fast. With technology advancing every day, the church faces a unique challenge: how do we respond? Do we resist the tide, or do we learn to surf?
Rather than seeing technology as a threat to tradition, I believe we should view it as a bridge. The church has a massive opportunity to embrace the digital world, not to replace our treasured traditions, but to amplify them. It is about becoming a community that adapts to the times while staying deeply rooted in its values.
Here is how we can navigate this balance.
Connection Beyond Sunday In the past, church communication was often limited to Sunday announcements or a printed bulletin. Today, digital tools allow the conversation to continue all week long.
Staying in Touch: Simple tools like messaging apps or email newsletters ensure no one misses out on events or urgent prayer requests. It keeps the pulse of the community beating between Sundays. Social Media as Ministry: It is not just about marketing; it is about reach. Platforms like Instagram or Facebook allow us to share daily reflections, Bible verses, or encouraging stories. It turns passive scrolling into a moment of spiritual connection. However, this comes with responsibility. We need to foster digital ethics—teaching our community to interact respectfully online, verify information before sharing, and protect privacy. The values we hold in the sanctuary should apply just as strictly to our online comments.
High Tech, High Touch There is often a fear that screens will replace the sacredness of worship. But when used wisely, technology actually enriches the experience.
Multimedia presentations, high-quality audio, and visual projections can make worship more immersive and accessible. They help engage a generation that is natively visual.
But here is the crucial balance: Technology should never replace physical presence. The intimacy of gathering together, shaking hands, and singing in the same room is irreplaceable. Digital tools are there to enhance that gathering, not substitute it. For those who cannot physically attend due to illness or distance, streaming provides a lifeline, but for the rest of us, it should encourage—not replace—face-to-face fellowship.
Conclusion The digital shift brings both challenges and opportunities. The goal isn’t to become a “tech church,” but to be an adaptive one. By using new tools wisely and ethically, we can preserve our traditions while making them accessible to a modern world. It is about using every available means to build a community that is inclusive, resilient, and connected—both online and offline.

A lot of parents worry about the games their children play. They are often afraid that some games might not be suitable for their kid’s age. But actually, parents need to know that every game already comes with an age rating set by the developers. These ratings exist to help parents decide if a game is okay for their children or not.
When making a game, developers and publishers already have a target audience in mind. They set the age rating based on what is inside the game—like violence, bad language, or adult themes. For instance, a game with intense fighting will have a higher age rating than a family-friendly game. Parents should treat these ratings as important guidelines, not just suggestions, to pick the right games.
International Age Rating Coalition (IARC) There is an organization called the International Age Rating Coalition (IARC) that connects different rating systems from around the world, including the US, Europe, and Australia. Their goal is to make sure parents and players get consistent advice on age-appropriate games.
One of the most famous systems is PEGI (Pan European Game Information). Used in most of Europe, PEGI rates games based on content like violence or bad words. The ratings go from age 3 (PEGI 3) up to 18 (PEGI 18).
Another popular one is the ESRB (Entertainment Software Rating Board), which is used in North America. It is quite similar to PEGI but uses categories like Everyone (E), Teen (T), and Mature (M). ESRB also explains why a game got that rating.
Indonesia Game Rating System (IGRS) Besides the international ones, Indonesia also has its own system called the Indonesia Game Rating System (IGRS). It was made to guide Indonesian parents and players about game content.
Right now, IGRS mostly covers games made by local developers. This means many big international games might not have an IGRS label yet. Popular hits like Fortnite, Call of Duty, or FIFA often don’t have an Indonesian rating to help parents decide.
Ideally, IGRS should expand to cover these international games too, since they are very popular here. This would give parents better information.
Even so, IGRS is a good start for raising awareness about game ratings in Indonesia. Parents can use IGRS for local games, but for now, it is a good idea to also check international ratings like PEGI or ESRB to get a complete picture before buying games for their kids.
Conclusion Understanding game ratings is the best way to protect children from content they shouldn’t see. Parents need to remember that every game has a rating from its creator, and this is a key tool for choosing the right titles. By looking at international systems like PEGI and ESRB, along with our local IGRS, parents can make smarter choices and ensure their kids play safely.

It feels like every time we blink, the world moves a little faster. Technology has fundamentally shifted how we learn, how we work, and how we talk to each other. We have accepted that smartphones keep us connected and streaming services bring entertainment to our living rooms.
But when it comes to our spiritual lives, the conversation gets a bit more complicated. Is there meaningful space for cutting-edge tech like Virtual Reality (VR) inside the church? It sounds like science fiction, but it is a reality we are already facing. I want to explore how these digital advancements might change the way we worship, interact with our community, and experience faith in a world that is increasingly glued to screens.
This isn’t about blindly accepting every new gadget, but rather looking at the future with curiosity. We need to think critically about how technology shapes us, even in our religious lives.
More Than Just Games First, let’s clear up what we are actually talking about. Virtual Reality (VR) often gets dismissed as a toy for gamers, but it is much more than that. It is part of a broader spectrum called Extended Reality (XR), which blends the physical and digital worlds.
The potential here is massive. In my own field of architecture, we use VR to let clients “walk” through a building before a single brick is laid. In education, students can take field trips to historical sites without leaving the classroom. The technology allows for immersion—a sense of “being there”—that a standard screen just cannot provide.
Worship in a Digital Space So, what happens when we bring this immersion into the church?
The most obvious application is accessibility. Imagine attending a service where you feel physically present in the sanctuary, even if you are sick at home or living in a different country. Unlike watching a YouTube stream where you are a passive observer, VR invites you to participate. You can look around, sing along, and feel a sense of shared space with other congregants.
It also breaks down geographical barriers. A “global church” becomes literal when people from different continents can gather in the same virtual room. Each person, represented by an avatar, can interact and engage in community in a way that feels surprisingly personal. Beyond Sunday service, this creates new avenues for pastoral care—offering counseling and support to people who might be intimidated by walking into a physical building.
Navigating the Challenges Of course, this isn’t a seamless transition. Integrating VR into church life brings real challenges that we have to talk about.
There are practical hurdles, like the cost of equipment and the technical learning curve. But more importantly, there are theological and social questions. Does meeting in a digital space dilute the communal experience? Is there a risk of isolating ourselves behind headsets instead of connecting face-to-face?
Attitudes vary wildly. Some see it as a mission field; others see it as a distraction. Both views have merit. Adopting VR shouldn’t mean discarding tradition. It is about finding a balance—figuring out where this technology adds value and where it might detract from the core mission of the church.
A Tool, Not a Replacement Technology will continue to shape our culture, whether the church participates or not. The goal isn’t to replace physical gathering—nothing can truly replace the warmth of a handshake or a shared meal—but to expand the reach of the community.
If we approach VR with an open mind and a critical eye, it can be a powerful tool. It allows us to visualize biblical stories in new ways, connect with isolated believers, and create worship experiences that are accessible to everyone. We don’t need to fear the future, but we do need to be intentional about how we build it.

Generative design is often talked about as a single concept, but in reality, it is a collection of distinct mathematical and computational techniques. For architects, these aren’t just abstract formulas; they are tools that allow us to explore design territories that human intuition alone might never reach.
By leveraging algorithms, we can push past simple geometry into complex, optimized forms. Here is a look at some of the most prominent techniques that drive this process.
Cellular Automata If you have ever heard of John von Neumann or Stephen Wolfram, you might be familiar with this concept. Cellular Automata (CA) operates on a grid of cells. Each cell looks at its neighbors and decides its next state based on a simple set of rules.
It sounds basic—simple rules governing simple cells—but the result is often surprisingly complex. Through iteration, these basic interactions evolve into intricate, emergent patterns. In architecture, we use CA to simulate how spatial configurations grow or to create dynamic façade patterns that respond to local conditions without needing a master blueprint for every single pixel.
Genetic Algorithms Inspired by the biological process of natural selection, Genetic Algorithms (GA) are essentially “survival of the fittest” for design.
Here is how it works: You define a set of parameters (the DNA) and a goal (fitness). The computer generates a population of designs, tests them against the goal, and “breeds” the best ones together, introducing random mutations along the way. Over thousands of generations, the design evolves. This is incredibly powerful for optimization—finding the most structurally efficient form or the perfect layout for energy performance that a human designer might take weeks to calculate.
Shape Grammar While Genetic Algorithms are about evolution, Shape Grammar is about language. It is a rule-based system where you define a vocabulary of shapes and a set of rules for how they can be combined or transformed.
Think of it as creating a “style guide” that the computer can execute. By establishing these geometric rules, architects can generate complex compositions that still adhere to a specific design logic or architectural language. It is particularly useful when you want to explore many variations of a design while keeping a consistent stylistic identity.
Expanding the Toolkit The field doesn’t stop there. The toolkit is constantly expanding with methods like Swarm Intelligence (based on the behavior of ant colonies or bird flocks) and Neural Networks (Deep Learning). Each brings a different strength to the table.
Generative design is more than just letting the computer “do the work.” It is about understanding which algorithm fits the problem at hand. Whether it is the biological logic of Genetic Algorithms or the rule-based structure of Shape Grammar, these tools allow us to partner with computation, merging our creative intent with the processing power to uncover unforeseen design possibilities.

The use of computers in the field of architectural design initially only involved digitizing tasks that were traditionally done manually. Computer-based modeling or drawing still relied on additive logic, which involved adding overlapped information without associative relationships, heavily relying on the designer’s consistency. This additive logic persisted for a long time as it was considered stable for exploring and refining variations through traditional image media. However, this logic had limitations as it lacked connections between depicted elements and couldn’t incorporate physically relevant aspects that shape the generation of real-world forms. These limitations prompted architects to develop their design mindset.
In 1963, a computer expert named Ivan Sutherland discovered a tool called the Sketchpad, which is considered the first CAD tool and served as a precursor to popular CAD computer applications in subsequent years. This marked the transition from additive logic to associative logic. Associative logic became the foundation for the use of computing in design, supported by the advancements in information technology and computer science.
In associative logic, the manipulation of shapes is performed directly, similar to how we draw a line on paper by moving our hand according to the desired line. However, when using associative logic in computer-based design, shape manipulation is achieved indirectly through algorithms. A line is not formed by the movement of our hand, but rather by calculating the distance between two points.
The architectural design process using computers is no longer limited to representational purposes; it harnesses the computer’s capacity to think and execute instructions based on procedures created by the architect. This approach is known as computational thinking, which has evolved alongside the increasing complexity and speed of computer capabilities. Computers can quickly generate shapes based on algorithms devised by architects, complemented by the architect’s logical thinking ability. The advantage of this approach is its ability to produce shapes that were previously challenging to achieve using conventional modeling techniques reliant on additive logic.
In general, computational thinking consists of four techniques:
decomposition
solving the problem by breaking the problem into several small problems.
abstraction
recognizing the key components of the differences in the problem to develop a solution to several problems.
pattern recognition
recognizing the similarity of components of a problem.
algorithm
a set of procedures to solve problems.
Computational design is a design process that leverages computational thinking. It has continued to evolve in the field of architectural design alongside the advancements in information technology, giving rise to various new terms such as parametric design, algorithmic design, and generative design.
